subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the failure of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration as disclosed in the agreement with Dimensional Investments Limited to protect the interests of the Sarnia band of Indians by entering into an agreement for the sale of Indian lands at approximately $2,000 an acre which were resold immediately to Ontario hydro at approximately three and a half times the price received by the Indians, resulting in an immediate profit to Dimensional Investments Limited of between $800,000 and $900,000.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member if he can inform me whether the agreement referred to has been tabled in the house?

subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I should like to have some assistance in this matter. Certain points occur to me to which I would ask members to direct their remarks. First, the matter of urgent public importance appears to involve the sale of the property of a band of Indians and therefore is somewhat local in character, affecting the property rights of certain individuals and not the public generally. Second, the question occurs to me whether this is an administrative responsibility. The Indian Act provides, of course, for jurisdiction over such matters by a minister of the government, but I am not familiar enough with the details to know whether the sale is one which is made by the Indians themselves or by the government. Then, of course, there is the further question of urgency of debate. My recollection is that this matter was extensively discussed in the press last week and earlier, and that may have a bearing on whether there is urgency of debate which would warrant the interruption of our proceedings.

subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could say a word on these points since I am asking leave-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I think I should hear the hon. member who is presenting the motion. Will he direct his remarks to the points I have raised, or any other arguments which he thinks support the motion?

subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
That is precisely what I was proposing to do. On the first point, whether this is a matter of national importance, of course the superintendent general of Indian affairs is a trustee for the Indians, and the sale was made by the minister, or by the crown, and the minister was agent for the crown. There can be, therefore, no question about this being an administrative responsibility of the government. It is true that the prior consent of the Indians has to be obtained, but the action is taken by the government, by the minister, and on the responsibility of the government. So I think there is no question about that.
I believe the disposal of any Indian lands in any part of the country is surely a trust the performance of which, as a national responsibility, is most urgent and most important. I could quote many eloquent statements on that point by the Prime Minister when he sat over here.

subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I had a lot of good examples when the hon. gentleman was the minister.

subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: The Prime Minister can speak, perhaps, when I am finished. But on the question of urgency-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: You seldom stop long enough for anyone else to speak.

subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
On the question of urgency, I may say there were articles in the press but I did not feel I could properly found my case on articles in the press. The hon. member for Trinity has sought for some considerable time to get the relevant document. The document was not tabled until Monday evening at approximately 10 o'clock. Had it been available on Friday I think we would have had no case, because the matter could have been brought up on the motion to go into supply. This opportunity having been denied us, and of course the minister's estimates having been completed, there is no opportunity to discuss the subject on her estimates. It did not appear to me there was any other opportunity to bring this matter up.
It is urgent in another way. I think it is urgent to know whether this high price which was paid by Ontario hydro was something the Indians lost or whether it was something that was done extravagantly by another government. This is important, in view of the fact that we live in a democratic country and certain decisions have to be made tomorrow. It seems to me that-

subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: The Prime Minister laughs as though elections were laughing matters, and as though the people were not entitled to be informed about public affairs before they vote.

subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I am not entering the argument, but the fact that an election is being held tomorrow in one of the provinces is not a matter of urgency in the House of Commons.

subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: On the Prime Minister's point, since the Prime Minister was permitted-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I would ask the hon. member who has the floor not to bring in provincial elections.

subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I think it is a matter of urgent importance to this house to know whether this land that was sold to Ontario hydro for $7,000 an acre was worth that, in which case the Indians should have got the $7,000, or whether it was not worth it. It is for that reason that it seems to me it is
Motion to Adjourn House urgent that this parliament, in this session, should have an opportunity to discuss this matter, and there is no other opportunity that I am able to see available under the rules.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate really let the cat out of the bag when he referred to the Ontario election tomorrow, and went on to say that this house should be able to deal with the question of whether or not another government has been extravagant.

subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: A breach of trust by this government.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: If he can succeed in moving the adjournment of the house on this occasion, then a day or two before the election in Alberta, which I think is on June 18, we may have another motion of the same kind. Surely this is reducing the rule for making motions of this kind to an absurdity. All the authorities clearly state that the debate itself must be urgent, and the only element of urgency in this matter is the Ontario election tomorrow.

subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Bl each of trust.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The hon. member also says there will be no other occasion on which to discuss this question. May I point out that we have one other supply motion. It will probably be called a week from Monday. I am sure the members of the government, including the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, will be delighted to discuss this subject should hon. members across the way have the courage to raise it then.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is in effect nothing more nor less than a propaganda motion and that the request made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is really not made in a very serious way.

subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the question of the Ontario election tomorrow is an extraneous matter and should be so considered by Your Honour. I believe the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) made an error of judgment when he advanced that as a reason for urgency of debate. I would suggest that there is urgency for debate on other and more substantial grounds. The urgency for debate is brought about not because there may be a motion to go into supply a week from Monday when, if it is the opinion of the official opposition at that time this is the most important matter on which to move, they may move in this field. Rather, it is an urgent matter because it brings the action of the government under a cloud.

Motion to Adjourn House It is an extremely serious charge that is alluded to in this motion that is being advanced. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration who is responsible, as has been pointed out, for giving permission for this land to be sold, tabled the agreement only Monday night. This is a motion that is being presented quickly thereafter in order to deal with the question, in order to get at the facts and see whether or not the Indians were denied money that should be theirs or whether for some other reason the Ontario hydroelectric commission paid a scandalous amount. These matters are urgent in that they should be dealt with and cleared up- if the government can clear them up-at this time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am prompted to enter this debate particularly because of some of the expressions of opinion by the leader of the house.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Before the hon. member proceeds I would remind him that it is not a debate. We are discussing the interpretation of the application of rule 26 to the specific points that were raised. I trust that he will not stray into the field of the provincial election.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of straying. I wish to deal with the three points Your Honour asked my friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate to deal with, but before dealing with them I thought it in order to tell the leader of the house that he was more persuasive in his arguments when he spoke as the Minister of Public Works than he is when he speaks as the new Secretary of State for External Affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: He was speaking as leader of the house.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
A moment ago he indicated that we lacked courage in not raising this matter on the motion for supply. It strikes me that if the government were courageous it would accept this invitation to adjourn the house and deal with the matter.
The points which Your Honour asked should be dealt with are the following. First, Your Honour asked for assistance in connection with the matter of the regional or national aspect of the debate. I think it is quite clear that because of the fact that the superintendent general of Indian affairs acts on behalf of all the Indians in this country, and not only on behalf of one of the bands, the matter becomes one of national interest rather than local interest.
Then it is quite clear on another point. The responsibility of the administration is such that when matters of this kind, such as sales

of land, are approved they must be approved by the governor in council, and the superintendent general in his responsibility as trustee must recommend to the minister approval of sales of this nature. In that respect I do not think there can be any doubt but that there is a responsibility as far as the administration is concerned.
I cannot agree with the argument by the leader of the house that this matter can be held over until a motion for supply is made, because there has been no indication as to when that is likely to come up, and the urgency of the debate lies in this fact, that the estimates of the hon. minister have been disposed of-

subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: What about the supplementary estimates?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I am asked from the rear, what about the supplementary estimates. Well,
I presume they will not come up until the end of the session, which may not be for two or three weeks. I presume that the ordinary estimates of the other departments would have priority, since the minister has already disposed of her estimates. So that is not an argument. The point of urgency is that there is no immediate opportunity to deal with a matter of this nature, which to me is allimportant because of the reason given by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate the exorbitant profits which have been made with regard to Indian lands, and for these reasons I suggest that the debate should be adjourned and this subject discussed.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
There are just one or two additional points I should like to make. I wish to refer, first, to the specific citation in Beauchesne regarding the question of whether a matter must be of national importance before it can be made the subject of such a motion as this. Your Honour has no doubt read paragraph 5 of citation 100 at page 90 of Beauchesne's fourth edition which says:
The adjournment of the house cannot he moved with reference to critical conditions generally prevailing in certain parts of the country.
It is clear from the motion that it relates to a specific and isolated sale. If there were allegations made with regard to the sale of Indian lands generally I should be prepared to admit that that was a matter of general application, but this motion is confined to a specific sale. I am not suggesting that this makes the content of the motion less important, but it certainly puts it outside the scope of the rule which must be observed before the adjournment of the house can take place at this time.
On the question of the urgency of debate, I would remind Your Honour that you have

to consider, it seems to me, two questions. The first is, is there any other way in which this matter could be discussed in the reasonably foreseeable future without the necessity of adjourning the house, and second, whether the necessity for dealing with the matter is so urgent that the house should immediately be adjourned.
May I remind Your Honour that a committee has recently been set up to review the Indian Act. I understand that that committee is holding a meeting today, and this would certainly provide another forum in which this question and others relating to the administration of the superintendent general of Indian affairs could be discussed.
It seems to me that this does dispose entirely of any suggestion that the house should be adjourned at this stage. Further, on the question of whether this matter requires to be dealt with now as one of urgency, may I remind Your Honour that this sale is' an accomplished fact. It is not as though the sale were about to be made and it was necessary, therefore, to discuss at this time whether or not it would be advisable to make it; or, from the point of view of hon. gentlemen opposite, to argue to prevent the sale. This sale, as I say, is an accomplished fact. There are other times at which it can be discussed, either in the committee or in this house on a supply motion or on the supplementary estimates. Since it is an accomplished fact, and with these other opportunities for debate being available, I submit that it clearly is not necessary to adjourn the house now in order to discuss it.
Thus on these three grounds-first, that it is a matter local in its import; second, that there are other occasions on which it can be discussed; and third, that the motion deals with an accomplished fact and is, therefore, not one which requires immediate discussion today-I submit that the motion is one which cannot be accepted.

speechtext: Perhaps I might be allowed to say a word about one of the points raised by the Minister of Justice. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SALE OF LAND, SARNIA  MOTION FOR ADJOURN- MENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I thank hon. members for a very complete and useful discussion of the application of rule 26 to this particular motion. If I might deal with the last point referred to-the suggestion of the Minister of Justice that as a joint committee is now dealing with the Indian Act it might be an answer to the motion-may I say that to my mind it seems that if the matter is one which comes under the rule it should be possible to bring it before the house itself.
It seems to me that the complaint is that certain property of a band of Indians has been sold for too little money, that the best price has not been obtained. I accept the proposition that it is the administrative responsibility of the department to do the best it can with these sales, just as it is its responsibility in connection with any sale or purchase of public property to get the

Motion to Adjourn House best price or pay the least price it can. That is a continuing responsibility. But this particular motion relates to a sale that has been completed, as was pointed out by the Minister of Justice. It is an accomplished fact. What the motion seeks to do is to criticize, condemn or question the government for having made the sale on the terms it did. It is more specifically a motion of censure of the government for something it has done.
Property rights are always important to the people involved, but I think the fact that this is a property matter involving property rights puts it in a different category from other motions we have had. It strikes me that if we were to allow the procedure of the house to be interrupted every time the administration of the government with respect to the sale or purchase of property was challenged it would open a very wide door and would tend to disrupt the proceedings of the house.
With respect to the rule that the matter must be of public importance and so pressing that the public interest will suffer if not given attention, subsections 2 and 5 of citation 100 of Beauchesne's fourth edition have been referred to, and perhaps this aspect is not so clear because the administrative action of the government is always a matter of general importance and in this case it relates to a fairly local occurrence.
In coming to the question of urgency of debate let me say this. As I have already said, this appears to be basically a motion of censure on the administration and would more properly be dealt with in that way. We could accomplish very little by debating whether the price is or is not adequate, and by a motion to adjourn the house we could not correct the situation. However, the matter is one which any hon. member of the house is entitled to bring up at an appropriate time.
Having regard to the fact that this sale has been a public issue for ten days-I am not sure when the sale price first became known-we were in debate on Monday night when we had a supply motion and airing of grievances; but I do not rest my decision on the timing of the filing of this document, I want to make that clear. The clerk reminds me that the sale was made some time ago. The urgency of debate seems to work against the mover of this motion.
There will be an opportunity shortly to discuss this matter. As it is not of such national scope and as the motion would not be corrective of anything which is pending except as a means of criticizing the government, it seems to me the opportunity should be taken when it can be taken on a later

occasion. I am not, therefore, prepared to accept the application for leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY STATEMENT ON PASSAGE OF UNITED STATES NAVAL SHIPS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport arising out of what I believe would be a very undesirable display of naval power by the United States in the St. Lawrence seaway if projected plans are completed. My question is this. Has the minister anything to report on his representations to the United States that the passage of United States naval vessels through the St. Lawrence seaway should be reduced to two a day? Would he care to comment on the story in this morning's press that the United States navy has announced that it will go ahead with plans as previously scheduled?

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY STATEMENT ON PASSAGE OF UNITED STATES NAVAL SHIPS
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. This morning I
asked the president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority to give me a report on this matter, and it is as follows.
Before the opening of navigation and in connection with arrangements for the royal visit our officials gained knowledge of the intended passage of United States naval vessels. At that time the size of the flotilla was not known and our immediate interest and concern, in discussion with the royal tour organization, was that the vessels would be so spaced as not to cause congestion at

the time of the official opening. It was our understanding that in so far as protocol was concerned, arrangements had been made between the United States state department and our Department of External Affairs. No one at that time could have foreseen the accumulation of shipping arising from the delayed opening of navigation due to ice conditions. Also, the influx of large ocean vessels was much greater than anticipated. Up to June 7, 248 ocean vessels passed through the Welland canal upbound as compared with 122 small ocean vessels up to the same date in 1958.
With the co-operation of the United States seaway corporation a meeting was held with United States naval officials at Ottawa on May 26 at which I outlined the situation at the Welland canal and requested that they report the same to their superior officers, with a view to considering preferably a reduction in the total number of vessels or, alternatively, the spacing of their movement over a longer period. At that time they replied that their plans had been practically completed and ships assigned, and that they could do no more than report the situation to their superior officers.
That is the end of the report of the president of the St. Lawrence seaway to me. When I was advised of the result of this meeting I discussed the situation with the United States ambassador on Friday, May 29, urging a reduction in the size of the flotilla and spacing of the ships at not more than two a day in order to minimize congestion. To this moment I have heard of no adjustment in the plans of the United States navy, though I was speaking to the United States ambassador about this matter as recently as one hour ago.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY STATEMENT ON PASSAGE OF UNITED STATES NAVAL SHIPS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I might direct a supplementary question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Is the minister prepared to discuss this matter with the government at Washington in an endeavour to avoid further unnecessary congestion of the St. Lawrence seaway when, in the words of the Minister of Transport, it is already congested far beyond anything that had been anticipated?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY STATEMENT ON PASSAGE OF UNITED STATES NAVAL SHIPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would be unfortunate indeed if the impression should go abroad either in Canada or in the United States that this matter is not being dealt with in a very friendly and considerate way by both governments. I might add one or two facts to the statement made by my colleague the Minister of Transport.
Under an agreement known as the Rush-Bagot agreement which dates back to 1817 66968-9-287
Inquiries of the Ministry it is necessary when one of the two countries wishes to bring a naval vessel into the great lakes to obtain the consent of the other country. There was an exchange of notes between Canada and the United States early this year with regard to the proposal of the United States navy to bring 28 naval vessels into the seaway. Canada agreed that this course could be followed. At that time, of course, no one realized the difficulties that would arise in getting the vessels through the Welland canal. I do not think either nation expected that there would be this tie-up and, of course, it affects the United States as well as Canada, so that everything has been done in good faith in connection with this proposal.
My department has made representations through the Canadian embassy in Washington, and I am very hopeful that some satisfactory method of solving the problem can be reached at a very early date.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY STATEMENT ON PASSAGE OF UNITED STATES NAVAL SHIPS

Whatever may be the difficulties which might follow from the numbers of the United States flotilla-that has been discussed by my colleagues-I would not want the idea to go forth that the hon. gentleman represented the views of the members of this house and of the people of Canada when he said "in view of the undesirable display of United States naval strength in the great lakes". That was a preamble unnecessary for the discussion of the objective nature of the question, and I want to make it perfectly clear that it does not represent, as I understand it and know it, the views of the Canadian people.

There is no doubt in our mind that when the agreement was made the circumstances were not at all the same as they are now. No one had any idea that the conditions would be such as they are, and in view of the fact that there is an undertaking in the Rush-Bagot agreement, I think all the minister can do is to make the necessary representations to the United States. I am sure that if they are done in the proper way, as the minister will unquestionably bring them forward, the United States will understand that there should be, if not a stoppage of the movement,

speechtext:
I should
like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. Would the minister care to comment on a Canadian Press report based on information attributed to officials of his department, in which it is stated that there are 70 million pounds of frozen pork in the possession of the government, and that in addition the government will have about 25 million pounds of canned pork on its hands by the end of June? Has the government any plans to dispose of these huge quantities of surplus pork?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF SURPLUS HELD BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to begin with I do not know where the newspaperman who wrote the article got his information, but his figures are not entirely accurate.
With respect to the allegation in the article that there is no storage space left to store pork and other products, I should like to point out that on May 1 public cold storage occupancy was approximately 83 per cent of capacity compared with 84 per cent in November of
Inquiries of the Ministry 1958. In other words, there was very little difference; in fact there was a little less than last November. The figure was higher than on May 1, 1958 when it was about 65 per cent. Cooler space occupancy was about the same on May 1 in both years.
As far as the disposal of pork is concerned, we have been selling some of the pork both in the local market and in the United States. We also have several deals pending for the sale of some of this pork abroad. In addition, during the months of July and August, as many hon. members are aware, the runs of hogs are very much reduced and we expect to move a considerable amount of this pork into consumption during the summer period.

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF SURPLUS HELD BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: When the minister says he intends to move this surplus pork into consumption, does he intend to move it into consumption in the Canadian market, and is this not likely to bring about a further depression of pork prices? I should also like him to comment on the further statement attributed to these officials that the 25 million pounds of canned pork will likely be given away.

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF SURPLUS HELD BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: I do not think there is any statement like the last one referred to by the hon. member in the press article which I read. In any event, officials of the department have no authority whatever to make any statement with respect to whether pork will or will not be given away, and I am sure that no such statements were ever made. The pork we hold in storage at the present time will be moved into the Canadian market during the summer months when, in nearly every year, the runs of hogs are not sufficient to meet the current demand.

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF SURPLUS HELD BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: May I ask a further question. Will this pork be placed on the Canadian market only if the price remains above the floor or at the floor?

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF SURPLUS HELD BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are selling this pork, and we have sold a certain amount already, at no cost to the stabilization board. In other words we are selling it at the price we paid for it plus the storage charges. We are going to continue to sell all the pork we can on that basis.
The hon. member stated that this procedure would cause a further depression in pork prices. There cannot be any further depression because the price is at the floor and has been at the floor for some considerable time. Naturally, any action we take to dispose of this pork is not going to put the price below the floor because we guarantee that.

Mr. Chairman, at the outset of this discussion on the main estimates of my department and the subagencies reporting to me I will, with your permission, spend a few minutes in summarizing, for the benefit of this committee, the more noteworthy items contained in our programs for 1959-1960.
The grand total of the several dozen appropriations, including statutory items, is $262,587,000, and that represents a slight increase of $1.1 million over the amount approved for the fiscal year 1958-59. From this it will be evident we will be maintaining the substantially accelerated tempo of last year's capital program, when we provided an additional $41 million. Maintenance of the proposed level of expenditure will enable us to perform many activities in such a way as to materially assist the country's economy and, at the same time, cope with the increasing demands from industry and the public generally in the field of transportation.
For the convenience of the members I intend to deal with the three main divisions of my department in the order of their appearance in the blue book. Before doing so, however, I wish to mention one general matter which is of special interest to all of us, namely the matter of our personnel establishment. Examination of the printed details in the estimates will show that the department is contemplating a total of 14,700 positions, either full-time or part-time, for this year. Although this represents a drop of 400 from last year, it does allow for transfer of 1,040 positions to the St. Lawrence seaway authority due to transfer of the main line canals. Thus it will be seen that in fact we are providing 640 additional positions in other sections of the department.

The main additions included in this figure are 114 for manning of new vessels; 240 in telecommunications because of the transfer to the department of the Northwest Territories and Yukon radio system and installation of new radio aids for aviation and marine at numerous additional sites; 167 to cope with the additional work load associated with general control of civil aviation, particularly air traffic control.
Budget planning for our canals section in the coming year will, of course, bear little resemblance to that of previous years. The combined requirements for operation and construction will total $3| million in comparison to last year's $11.5 million. The only sizeable projects pertain to the Canso canal, where some $0.5 million will be spent on a mooring wall and fenders. Apart from the general votes a special appropriation of $3 million is included this year to cover the estimated operating deficit on non-toll canals transferred to the seaway authority, that is to say the Lachine, the Sault Ste. Marie canals and the remaining portion of the Cornwall canal, as well as capital expenditures on these canals and the second Welland canal.
One of our departmental responsibilities which continues to expand is that of marine steamer operation. Especially is this so in our work of co-ordinating the movement of cargo required for normal government resupply and for Canadian and United States military installations in the far north. During 1958 that tonnage totalled 78,000 tons, or double the 1957 volume. All planning associated with operations and building in the Arctic must be hedged with some uncertainty because of the extraordinary factors to be considered. For this reason it is difficult to anticipate transportation needs. However, we do believe there will be no lessening of the volume transported by water last year.
I am indeed happy to refer to the takeover in 1959 by my department of the last segment of the sea supply for the D.E.W. line. In 1958 the government, through the agency of Northern Transportation Company, took on the resupply of those stations in the central region, and my department became co-ordinator for the Foxe basin area. The United States government agencies with which we worked expressed unqualified approval of the capability displayed by Canadian resources and equipment, both governmental and commercial. As a result we have reached agreement that the department will extend its responsibility to the last segment, that is those radar stations on the east coast of Baffin island. Before leaving this item I do wish to
Sup p ly-Transport
pay tribute to the splended co-operation we have received from the various United States government agencies involved.
On the capital side, our marine steamers' fiscal requirements will fall off somewhat, not because of a decrease in physical volume but rather because several of the large items will be in either the planning stage or the completion stage. Before the 1959-60 fiscal year expires we expect work should be virtually completed on several new or replacement units, such as three supply and buoy vessels, which will operate from ports in the Atlantic provinces; a diesel electric icebreaker for service on the eastern seaboard and in the eastern Arctic; an icebreaker-supply ship type for the west coast and Arctic; a number of service vessels which will enable us to release obsolete units operated for many years on the St. Lawrence river; and autoferry vessels which will service Bell island, Newfoundland, and Pelee island, Ontario.
During the past year departmental officials, in collaboration with Canadian National Railways, have made a thorough study of ways and means of improving the Newfoundland coastal steamship services, which have been hampered by the shortage and inadequacy of vessels employed, the insufficiency of berthing space, storage areas, etc. In view of the findings thus made the government has decided to construct additional passenger-cargo vessels. The estimates now before this committee include the sum of $2,300,000 toward the cost of two of these vessels, and I expect a third to be added in next year's estimates. In addition, the Department of Public Works will commence the construction of freight sheds and wharf improvements at Corner Brook and Lewisporte, and vote 416 contains approximately $800,000 for this purpose.
Continuation of the program, under way for the past few years for modernization of our marine agency depots will be pushed along this year. The expenditures related thereto will form the largest single type of commitment in vote 402, which will differ very slightly in size. We are planning on a reduced financial outlay for the St. Lawrence ship channel service. Capital commitments pertaining to general improvement of the channels in the St. Lawrence and Saguenay rivers will be unchanged, but our maintenance dredging proceeded at an extraordinary rate in 1958 and a reduction is therefore expected. This, however, will be temporary only, since this work has been held back during construction of the seaway, and needs to be expanded again if the channel from Montreal is to be improved as required.

Supply-Transport
At this point I come to the air services of the department, for which we are budgeting more than 60 per cent of our proposed departmental fiscal outlay. Administration and operation of the telecommunications branch which, among other responsibilities, maintains the hundreds of air and marine navigational aids throughout Canada, will require a sum very close to the $17 million mark. In dealing with the staffing problem I have already alluded to certain heavy assignments we must add to this work load.
There is one other major item. I refer to the proposed purchase of four Decca navigator chains to assist marine navigation on the eastern seaboard. Evaluation studies carried out during the past two years have demonstrated the value of this navigation system, especially in periods of poor visibility.
Our responsibilities in the circle of international communications will require our technical officers to devote a good deal of their time and effort to work associated with a number of important meetings. During 1959 the international telecommunications union, an agency of the United Nations, will have a conference in Geneva to revise the convention of 1952. In addition there will be a radio conference in Geneva to revise the international radio regulations which cover many vitally important matters, such as frequency allocations.
In the area of radio aids construction and acquisition of equipment, we are contemplating the expenditure of $14 million. Five years ago the department inaugurated a program for combining marine and aeronautical stations in order to avoid duplication of manpower and equipment. One of the new stations will be at the new Prince Rupert, B.C. airport on Digby island. The other station to be replaced is the historic station on Signal hill, St. John's, Newfoundland, at which point Marconi received his first transAtlantic radio message.
Another noteworthy part of the year's program is the emphasis we will be giving to the development of radio and electronic systems to assist air traffic control communications by extending the distance over which a controller in an air traffic centre may talk directly to a pilot.
So much for the telecommunications branch. I shall now deal briefly with the meteorological branch. Too often we find that the public mistakenly think of the meteorological service in terms of public weather forecasting only. That, of course, is one of the important functions, but it is only one of many. Special weather forecasting is performed for shipping in the Atlantic and Pacific coastal waters, great

lakes, St. Lawrence river, etc. Air navigation, both civil and military, in all sections of the country, as well as over the Atlantic, Pacific and polar regions, depends heavily on the advice of the weather expert. The agricultural, forestry and transportation industries rely extensively on the findings of research endeavours performed on their behalf.
One of the very interesting activities to which special attention will be given this year is related to preparation of forecast charts at various levels of the atmosphere. The objective there will be the development of methods of preparing these charts by numerical means using highspeed electronic computers. The appropriation for operation of the branch will also this year contain an item of $370,000 to cover aerial ice survey. In previous years the Royal Canadian Air Force performed a considerable amount of the Arctic flying for this purpose, but the over-all requirement has grown to the point where it is deemed advisable to turn over the work to commercial operators. The reconnaissance will range from the lower St. Lawrence and gulf area as far north as the Arctic archipelago.
Finally I shall touch on the civil aviation requirements. Our national investment in facilities and equipment provided for the use of those who travel by air is indeed most substantial. The adoption of faster aircraft, the steady upward climb in traffic, the development of the more remote areas of our country, and the constant demands from the public generally, commercial interests and public officials, for more and better airways, airports, etc., all make inevitable some increase in expenditures for maintenance and operation. We are therefore expecting that the numerous items of costs for these purposes will be approximately 17 per cent higher than those of last year. Some $365,000 additional will be needed to defray maintenance costs for new or enlarged air terminals. Several millions of the increase arise from new or broadened tasks allocated to the department at a considerable number of isolated or semi-isolated locations such as Fort Nelson, Whitehorse, Goose Bay and Frobisher, where costs of materials, transportation, salaries, messing, repairs and upkeep and the like are so much higher.
It has been decided that the Department of Transport will take over operation and maintenance of the United States air force airstrip at the Cambridge bay station in 1959. I might add that we are continuing to give consideration to the possibility of a similar

take-over at other sites in subsequent years such as Cape Dyer, Hall lake, Cape Parry, Tuktoyaktuk.
The function we perform with regard to air traffic control along our airways, and especially in the vicinity of airports, is another case in point. Last year I reported an increase of 25 per cent here. For 1959-60 we have succeeded in levelling off to an appreciable degree; none the less some $350,000 extra must be provided. On this segment of our supervisory responsibility the advent of the jet age has a particularly telling effect, for it means the testing, purchase and operation of a dozen and one types of expensive electronic devices. Here in Canada we are as yet still on the threshold, and we will not begin to feel the real impact until 1960 when our first commercial jet transports enter the picture.
In establishing the level of our 1958-59 construction program to meet civil aviation requirements it was necessary for parliament to apportion to the related vote a sum of money which represented an increase of 80 per cent. On February 5 of this year when the Minister of Finance tabled the main estimates, he explained that this program would remain at the same high level. Nevertheless we are providing some $600,000 more for administration of this service. Those two statements-the same level of activity but sharply increased administrative costs-do appear rather contradictory. The explanation lies in a decision of treasury board that partial costs of air traffic control and related services previously recovered from national defence should in future be absorbed by the transport appropriation.
In the time at my disposal I could not hope to single out what might be considered the large expenditures. This vote totals $63 million and of the hundreds of items-and I use the term "hundreds" intentionally, because the list runs to more than 50 pages -many certainly come under the category of "large". I will therefore confine my remarks to some general observations about our program.
Present expectations are that within the next year we should be able to complete, or almost complete, major terminal construction at such places as Halifax, Montreal, Gander and Ottawa. In addition, very substantial progress will be made on new terminals at a number of other points, Regina, Winnipeg and Toronto, to mention a few. Upwards of $15 million is earmarked for miscellaneous work; for example, new airports at Three Rivers and Sherbrooke; new runways; improvements to existing runways; taxiways; buildings for ancillary services, etc. at dozens of airports from coast to coast.

Mr. Chairman, in concluding my remarks I should like to say I fully appreciate the somewhat sketchy nature of my statement. I would hope, however, that hon members will likewise appreciate that the very diversity of my department's responsibilities and operations makes it difficult to report in more detail. I trust, too, that my statement will be of assistance to them in their consideration of our estimates.

Mr. Chairman, I think the committee will, on the whole, be appreciative of the comprehensive report which the minister has given on the activities of the various branches of his department. After all, the Department of Transport is one of the most important, if not the most important in the government service, and it would have been unfortunate if the minister had not seen fit, as he has done on at least two occasions in the past, to bring forward a detailed statement concerning some of the things which have happened during the course of the year and some of the projects which he has in mind for the future.
However, I may tell the minister without any hesitation that I am keenly disappointed in the fact that there are two matters at least which were not dealt with in his statement. I had some occasion to refer to the first of these matters the other evening. It seems to me that there should be made today an over-all statement by the minister in connection with the operation of the St. Lawrence seaway, and I am sorry that the hon. gentleman has not yet seen fit to make such a statement.
As the committee knows, there have been some obstacles and difficulties; there has been a great deal of misunderstanding, and unfortunate publicity has been given to the seaway, first, at the end of last season when all those ships were cluttered up in the ice in the Lachine canal and in Montreal harbour; next, at the opening of navigation, when because of difficulties arising from ice conditions navigation had to be postponed, and finally because perhaps-and I hope this is a fact-an inordinate number of new ships entered the canal. All this goes to show that the success of the operation is, as 1 believe, assured, but I hope the minister will take the committee into his confidence and tell us the whole story about the present position from the entrance to the seaway at Montreal right up to the head of the lakes.
There are two serious bottlenecks. There is the one at Welland which was mentioned here the other evening. I know I need not tell the minister this, but when I was near Lancaster for a public ceremony less than a week ago there were no fewer than 25

ships waiting at anchor to enter the Eisenhower lock. I should not have said "Lancaster"; it was in the vicinity of Glen-walter in the county of Glengarry. These ships were tied up because of conditions that existed further down the river.

I am sure he would agree that it takes at least one navigation season, if not more than one, to ascertain whether the facilities are adequate to meet the traffic, and I invite him now, as I did the other evening, to make such a statement at the first opportunity.

This morning on orders of the day I once again raised the question of United States naval vessels, 27 in number, entering the St. Lawrence seaway toward the end of June. In the introductory preamble to my question I said I considered this an undesirable display of United States naval power. Although two members of the government replied to the question, the Prime Minister seized the opportunity of grabbing these words and making his own comments. After the Prime Minister sat down the hon. member for Laurier very appropriately said that since more comprehensive remarks had been made on this question he would like to make some comments of his own. When the hon. member for Laurier sat down I claimed the floor. The Speaker decided to ask the house whether I would have unanimous consent in order to make some comments and hon. members on the government side refused that consent when the question was put.
I regret that action on their part. I believe it was most unfair and discourteous. I doubt if there is anything very much for them to gain by acting in that way. I repeat, however, what I said before, namely that it would be a great error to have this United States naval flotilla coming into the seaway toward the end of June, although arrangements had been made previously by agreement with the Canadian government, and although it is understandable that many people in the United States and some people in Canada would like to see this tremendous display when the President of the United States and the Queen are here. Under the economic circumstances surrounding the St. Lawrence seaway at this time it would be a great error for 27 ships to present themselves at the seaway and delay the commercial use of the seaway for a number of days and, as has been said by people who understand the operations of the seaway, probably cause the type of congestion and tie-up which would take some weeks to unravel.
In his comments on the orders of the day the Prime Minister referred to the United States as a friendly nation. Well, of course, that is correct. The United States is a friendly nation, and we have friendly agreements with the United States. We have friendly discussions with them and I would suggest that, as two friendly nations discussing this question, the United States should give sympathetic consideration to the request now made by the Canadian government that the size of the flotilla should be reduced at any rate when it goes through the seaway.
The United States authorities, probably standing on rather firm legal grounds or technical grounds in the sense that a prior

Supply-Transport
agreement had been arrived at between Canada and the United States, takes the position that these 27 ships should proceed. But notwithstanding that prior agreement, notwithstanding that the Canadian government made a very serious error in judgment as far as the condition of the St. Lawrence seaway is concerned at the present time, as the minister said earlier today, I think there should be a reduction in the number of ships passing through. Undoubtedly if the Canadian government had known about the congestion that was to take place in the seaway this agreement never would have been entered into.
Canadian shippers of iron ore, Canadian shippers of grain, Canadians generally whose livelihood depends on the efficient use of the seaway will resent very greatly any interference with its operation which results in economic disadvantage to themselves and economic dislocation to the country through a display that is not necessary. Although the hon. member for Laurier may amend his remarks of the other evening, I think he was correct when he said the flotilla should stop at Montreal and should not proceed through the seaway.
There have been great disappointments in the operation of the seaway. People who depend on the seaway for the shipment of iron ore and other Canadian products are coming to the conclusion that unless suitable action is taken the St. Lawrence seaway will net result in a saving in costs as had been anticipated. I hold in my hand a great many statements, statements for example by men like T. R. McLagan, president of Canada Steamships, saying that our Canadian products should have priority in going through the seaway, and that unless steps were taken to provide such priority increased costs would result.
There has been a very serious bottleneck at the Welland canal, and consideration has been given to providing twin locks and taking other measures to provide a more efficient seaway. The seaway has been built at great cost to this country. The seaway authority can now spend some $335 million, as authorized by parliament and although this is a much larger sum of money than it was originally expected it would be necessary to spend there is no assurance whatever, as far as I can see, that this amount will do the job and result in the completion of the seaway.
There have been many reports of congestion; there have been many reports of difficulty in navigating the locks; there have been many reports of inefficiency, of serious errors having been made in the construction of the seaway. A few weeks ago it was my privilege to be taken by a longtime friend of mine, who

is himself an engineer and worked on the seaway for a considerable length of time, to view the various locks and facilities around Montreal. On examination although, of course, I do not claim to have any particular knowledge of the seaway-
Since I came to parliament this is the first thing I have heard the hon. member say he did not know.

I appreciate that compliment from my hon. friend.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, at one o'clock I had been saying that I had the opportunity a few weeks ago to visit the St. Lawrence seaway in the vicinity of Montreal and to inspect the various locks in that area. I also said that I was in the company of an engineer who had been an inspector on the seaway itself. One needs only to glance over the sides of the St. Lambert locks, the Cote St. Catherine locks and the Beauharnois locks to see the huge bulges in the walls. These bulges appear to extend out about eight inches, and this is an almost unbelievable error in engineering and construction. This situation does not apply merely to one of the locks but is a consistent fault in almost all of the locks to which I have referred.
There has been a great deal of reference to boats striking the sides of the locks. If the eight inch bulges were not there boats could and undoubtedly would still scrape the sides but I am certain that because of these eight inch bulges on either side the likelihood of boats striking the walls as they go through the locks is increased. There are steel guards along the locks in sections about three feet long which are supposed to be bolted together. There is provision for a bolt to bind one guard to another. In a great many instances the bolts are not there at all and instead of the guards coming closely together they are a quarter of an inch or perhaps as much as half an inch apart. It was pointed out to me that as cables are used to draw vessels along it is quite possible from time to time for the cables to get caught in the spaces between the guards. The spaces are there at least in part because the bolts are missing that were to be used to connect the guards.
As one might expect, the gates are huge. They are called mitre gates. Again, it was pointed out to me that unlike other gates there is only one mitre on these gates. The

mitre is at the top and when the gates come together the mitre at the top assures that their closing will be synchronized and that they will come together correctly and in line. But with only one mitre at the top it has been stated that logs that have gone to the bottom could become jammed in the gates at the bottom and thus spring the gates, and the springing of the gates could cause very serious difficulty for the seaway.
I was also informed that the spare gates which are in the walls and supposed to be available for use cannot be used because the facilities to move them are not available and therefore for the time being at least the spare gates cannot be used. When the gates are shut they are to be relatively watertight. I believe that to mean that there may be some sweating and some very minor leakage of water when the gates are closed, but what it does not mean is that water will spurt through the gates. Some of the gates do not admit as much water as others but in some cases water is spurting through the gates. Water is coming up from the bottom a distance of three or four feet, I would judge from looking down, which means that the spurts of water come out under a great deal of pressure.
It was pointed out to me that as the end of navigation approaches and freezing weather sets in the leaks in the gates will bring about a substantial accumulation of ice which in turn will have to be knocked off and will make the seaway facilities more difficult to use. I was also informed that the bolts in the gates are in many instances one-sixteenth of an inch smaller than the holes in which they are placed. The difference between the size of the bolt and the hole in which it is placed allows water to leak around the bolts and this could also be a source of substantial trouble in the future.
In addition to the substantial quantities of water coming through the gates when they are closed, when the gates have been opened and the water has left the lock and the gates are being shut again one can see water coming up between the cement reinforcement blocks against which the gates are shut. Generally these substantial blocks of cement are in two sections and water can be seen coming through at the place where the two blocks fit together. Moreover, in the upper Beau-harnois lock one can see water shooting up through the cement itself in the reinforcement blocks to which I have referred. In fact, the cement appears to be quite porous in that particular lock. If these reinforcement blocks are so porous as to allow water to come up through the cement I am certain that their life will indeed be limited.

Perhaps on a project of this magnitude it is inevitable that some faulty construction will appear but I understand that the faults to which I have referred were pointed out by the inspection authorities and that steps were not taken to correct them. If this is the situation, I think it is a very serious one and I believe there should be a very full inquiry into the matter.
I am suggesting that, although the government has refused it in the past, there should be a full inquiry by a House of Commons committee into the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway, into those very substantial faults that appear, and that there should be brought before that committee competent engineers who are acquainted with the seaway to testify as to why this faulty construction exists and to what extent it, in fact, endangers the life of the seaway.
The hon. member for Vancouver East placed a question on the order paper some time ago dealing with the construction of the Cornwall island high level bridge. The answer to question No. 5 is rather important. Question No. 5 reads:
Are the river piers of the Cornwall bridge down to bedrock? If not, what is the distance from the bottom of the piers to bedrock on (a) the Canadian side; (b) the American side?
The answer is found on page 935 of Hansard for February 11, 1959, and is as follows:
No, the piers were designed for and are founded on extremely dense glacial till.
Main pier, No. 12-(a) west shaft, 20.1 feet; east shaft, 19.7 feet.
Main pier. No. 11-(b) west shaft, 23.8 feet; east shaft, 23.9 feet.
This huge bridge, built at a cost of many millions of dollars, has piers which are not down to bedrock but merely placed on dense glacial till. I wonder why the extra expense was not incurred to put the piers down to bedrock? I am informed again that the cost of putting the piers down to bedrock would have been a relatively few thousand dollars compared with the many millions of dollars that were spent in the construction of this bridge. In reply to the hon. member for Vancouver East, there was further information given to show that there was a movement in one of the piers. I quote:
Cable-bent pier No. 13-top of west shaft-easterly i inch and southerly \ inch; Top of east shaft-westerly l inch and southerly 1 inch.
This shows the movement of the piers, and again I am informed that movement arises out of the fact that the piers were not put down to bedrock. I feel, Mr. Chairman, that there should be a full inquiry into the construction of the Cornwall bridge, that there should be a full inquiry by a committee of this house as to whether or not the bridge

S up p ly-Transport
is, in fact, properly constructed and whether or not it is a bridge that will last the normal length of time it would have been expected to last if it had been built down to bedrock.
I am told, once again by an engineer, that this bridge is doomed because the piers are not on bedrock but are on glacial till and cannot last the length of time that would be expected to be the normal life of that bridge. Mr. Chairman, that is a very strong statement, that statement I think coming from a man who was connected with the seaway, not the Cornwall bridge in particular but with the seaway, is one that warrants the most thorough investigation. If this bridge has been constructed in a faulty manner, this committee should inquire as to whether or not the bridge is, in fact, safe.

seen-he has seen a lot of things-the contract which was entered into between the seaway authority and all the contractors which provides for the construction to be completed in accordance with the plans and specifications?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the minister whether he is going to reply to the questions which I put to him before the luncheon recess?

Yes, I should be glad to do so. First of all, the hon. member for Laurier asked for a report on the operation of the seaway to date. I expect to be making in the not too distant future a report on the seaway authority and I feel that a little bit more time is required in order properly to assess the operation of the seaway, it being a little bit too early to make a proper assessment at the present time. With regard to the operation of the locks and so on, they are being studied very carefully and their operation compared to the operation of the United States locks or at least with the Eisenhower and Snell locks, which of course are United States locks, in order to see whether our locks are operating as well as theirs. As the hon. member knows, they have been in operation for a longer period of time than ours.
As to the Welland canal, as I have mentioned in this house already, we are examining all possible means of speeding up the operation of the canal. Specific matters that we are examining are possible construction of mooring walls between certain of the locks, and also a comparison is being made of the time taken in opening and closing lock gates at Welland as compared with the time taken to operate other lock gates in the new section of the seaway, down in the St. Lawrence section.
With regard to the other matter which the hon. member raised, namely the question of the land expropriations at Malton, I have jotted down a few points which I think would be of interest to him and to the committee. They are as follows. When I assumed office I found that while the great majority of the land expropriation cases at Malton had been settled, there were a number which had been outstanding for a long time. The department had had several different valuations made by individual appraisers, as well as by the departmental real estate staff. However, the
Supply-Transport
member from that area quite sincerely believed that the valuations made and received by the department were too low and urged a further valuation. In view of the sincere belief of the member of parliament concerned that these valuations were too low and were unfair to his constituents, I felt that it was desirable that there should be a further appraisal made, and I agreed that this should be done. I also assured the hon. member that the results of this further valuation would be studied with the greatest care not only by my own officials but by officials of treasury board as well, in order to ensure that it got the fullest possible consideration. I did not go beyond that.
I was satisfied with the real estate qualifications of the individual who was suggested to me by the member from the area for the purpose of this appraisal and his services were retained. When his report was received it was studied in great detail by officials of my department and by officials on the staff of treasury board, as I had undertaken. Both were of the opinion that the valuations submitted were too high, and should not be accepted by the federal government. I made no formal submission or recommendation of these valuations to treasury board but, as the hon. member for Laurier knows, it is quite customary for matters to be discussed informally, both with treasury staff and at the board itself, without formal recommendations having been submitted; and this is just what happened in this case. Since both my department and treasury board felt that these valuations could not be accepted, the matter was allowed to proceed in the exchequer court in the manner provided by law.

Mr. Chairman, when, in 1957, I made my maiden speech in this house, I urged the government to build this railway line between Matane and Gaspe. I mentioned the matter again in 1958, and I am proud to raise it again today.
As I was saying a moment ago, we have a great wealth of natural resources, as well as qualified workers in Gaspe. Our young people are strong and, what is more important, they have pluck. There are many good sites for new industries, but investors are not taking any chances, because there are no means of transportation. The northern part of the Gaspe peninsula is completely isolated.

In 1959, at a time of prosperity and of high technical progress, barges are still being used to carry goods from Montreal or Quebec, and they can be used only in the navigation season, which lasts 4 to 5 months. That is a striking and dangerous inconsistency for the economic life of that part of the country, and also for the family life of its people. Having to find work elsewhere in order to support his family, a father has to spend a large part of the year away from his wife and hardly ever sees his children. The children, left only to the care of the mother, often leave home at a very early age. It is easy to realize the moral responsibility of the government in the face of such chaos.
The authorities realize this, they are aware of the situation, and if I raise the matter again it is because I know that something can be done and, I hope, will be done. I want each of my honourable colleagues to know that my constituency, which stretches over a distance of 320 miles and is populated by large families, is not seeking any favours. However, it wants to share in the general prosperity of this great country, and it is calling out loudly, sometimes desperately, for its due. My constituents will feel they have largely received their share when a railway is built between Matane and Ste Anne des Monts.
Oh, Gaspesians are patient alright. Indeed, they have been asking for this railway for 20 years. For 20 years, the previous administrations have considered the matter as insignificant. However, the people of Gaspe showed that their patience can reach a limit, and placed their trust in the Conservative party. I know that this government, and particularly the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees), will see that this problem is settled, and I do hope it will be soon.
I do not believe that Mr. Gordon, for whom
I	have great respect, can decide whether a railway is important or not for the Gaspe peninsula. Members are elected to point out to the government the needs of their constituents. If action on this project is left to the bureaucrats, the member's prestige will suffer, and I know that such is not the intention of the present government.
Before closing, I must also commend the government, and particularly the Minister of Transport, for the improvements made to the railways between Matapedia and Gaspe. Up to 1957, a trip between those two points took
II	hours, whereas the same trip now takes six
Supp ly-Transport
hours. The train is always filled with passengers, and I am sure the Canadian National Railways is not losing money on it. I hope that, by 1960, I shall be able to rise again in this house, not to press for this railway, but to thank the government for carrying out a project that is dear to the hearts of the member and the people of Gaspe, namely, the construction of a railway linking Matane and Ste Anne des Monts.

Mr. Chairman, I have no wish to delay the passing of these estimates, but I would like to deal with an urgent issue. On behalf of the municipal authority and the citizens of Repentigny, I would ask the Bell Telephone Company of Canada to put in the extended sector service in the town of Repentigny, one of the most progressive collectivities in the federal riding of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm.
Mr. Chairman, the municipal authorities of Repentigny, the chamber of commerce and the citizens' association, have, on many occasions, approached the Bell Telephone Company of Canada asking it to grant, as far as possible, the service asked by the people of that progressive locality. Mr. Chairman, the Bell Telephone Company of Canada is treating Repentigny as if it were an underdeveloped locality. I would not like that company to think that this town is part of a Colombo plan country, but it is located in Canada, i.e. in a wealthy progressive country which is setting the pace for the whole world in this field.
At this time in Repentigny, almost 400 subscribers of the telephone company still use the crank-up telephone, a 30 year old gadget. The company goes on multiplying users of a single line and we are now up to 16 on the same one, which, in this case, can, indeed be called a party line.
Mr. Chairman, the Bell Telephone Company of Canada is a public service corporation which has to keep abreast of the progress of towns like Repentigny. The company has made an $11 million profit during the first quarter of 1959, i.e. $3 million more than in the same period of 1958. Company profits have gone up from $7,299,118 in 1946 to $29,146,855 in 1956. Those revenues are, as a matter of fact, only apparent ones, for the real profits are much more considerable. The company has increased its depreciation reserves to $247,347,199 and its deferred taxation reserves to $58,133,562.
The Bell Telephone Company of Canada has practised automation on a high scale

Supply-Transport
reaping enormous profits. Telephone subscribers should also benefit accordingly.
Before concluding, may I be allowed, Mr. Chairman, to read out, or to give the substance of a brief submitted by the chamber of commerce of Repentigny to the president of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. These are the points made to the company by the Repentigny chamber of commerce:
(a)	the chamber of commerce considers that by the crank up telephone service part of the town of Repentigny is isolated from the rest of the locality within the same territorial limits from the public site known as the Chateau du Fleuve;
(b)	The chamber of commerce considers that there is complete confusion in the telephone service, because that part of the town has to communicate through the St. Paul l'Ermite central to speak with another point within the same town of Repentigny and that moreover, in order to communicate with subscribers living east of the town, it is necessary to resort to long distance service.
(c)	The chamber of commerce considers that the Repentigny central should be autonomous, and that causes for discrimination within the limits of one and the same municipality should disappear.
(d)	The chamber of commerce considers that the town of Repentigny should enjoy direct service with Montreal, like other municipalities in the area which have such service;
(e)	The chamber of commerce considers that its territory is definitely situated within the 15 mile radius, and that every effort should be made to admit this geographical fact, rather than to attempt to evade the issue by any means, either by dealing with it from the point of view of "central to central", "sub-branch", or any other angle which does not agree with the facts.
(f)	The chamber of commerce feels it is very easy and even necessary to set up any telephone central on Bourdon Island;
(g)	The chamber of commerce considers that a study should be made and reports submitted on the possibility of using the cable facilities as they exist on the LeGardeur de Repentigny bridge (there are 12 of them, we are told).
Mr. Chairman, that problem has been existing in the town of Repentigny for some years. The town of Repentigny has enjoyed extraordinary development in recent years. It has residences of great value and, once again, after all representations made by your humble servant, by the authorities and associations of that town, I ask, once and for all, the Bell Telephone Company of Canada to settle that problem in order that the progress of that town in the federal constituency of Joliette-L'Assomption-Mont-calm, be not paralyzed.

Therefore, without casting any reflection on him, I will say that one of the peremptory statements he made was to the effect that in his opinion, there was no railway extension which deserved more sympathy and a more generous study than that of my hon. friend because, he said, he believed in a national development program for Canada, and the building of that railway was one of the projects which should be contemplated.
