speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I want to turn to another problem which is of importance to me and I think to the committee generally, but before I do that I will not take the opportunity of attempting to reply to what was said by the hon. member for Assiniboia although I could deal with the matters which he raised because I had some association with them in the early stages. I think I shall leave that to the minister who is much more capable than I am to deal with it because he has the facts at his disposal, and I do hope that before the first item of his estimates is disposed of he will deal with the charges that were made.
I rose to deal with another matter affecting the St. Lawrence seaway, namely one which has to do with the development of power and navigation in the Lachine section. It is not only of importance to those who live in the metropolitan area of Montreal but it is, I know, of importance to the officers of the St. Lawrence seaway authority and those of the Department of Transport. I refer now, of course, to the joint development of navigation facilities and power facilities in the Lachine section. As the house knows, the seaway authority proceeded to develop navigation facilities in the Lachine section independently of power following approval of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act in 1954 and thereafter. This is a matter which has engaged the attention of the public
Supply-Transport
for some time in the Montreal area and I shall attempt to deal with it as objectively as I can.
It has recently been stated that the Quebec government had good reasons for not carrying out the development in conjunction with the St. Lawrence seaway authority; that had Quebec proceeded with the development of power at Lachine the cost would have been far in excess of what it will be if Quebec goes ahead alone, and that this decision is based upon the opinion of qualified hydro experts. That is not what the qualified experts of Quebec hydro thought for a long time and, as a matter of fact, over a long period of years.
In 1948 the government of Canada established what was known as a board of engineers to deal with the improvement of the Lachine section of the St. Lawrence waterway. The board was composed of distinguished engineers, Mr. R. A. C. Henry, then chairman of the air transport board; Dr. T. H. Hogg, who was at one time chief engineer of Ontario hydro; Dr. Arthur Surveyer, an outstanding engineer in the city of Montreal; Mr. Guy Lindsay and Mr. C. W. West, then employees of the Department of Transport. At the time of this report the engineers who made the report asked the experts of Quebec hydro for their opinion on this whole matter and Quebec hydro undertook to organize an enginering staff to carry out the investigations necessary for the preparation of estimates covering a combined navigation and power project.
As a result, Quebec hydro after extensive studies submitted five different projects for the consideration of the board and the board, after reviewing these projects and in consultation with the representatives of Quebec hydro, selected two projects for power development which embodied the best features of the five projects submitted, either of which would provide the navigation facilities required and permit full utilization of the power available. The estimates of cost prepared by the engineers of Quebec hydro were adopted by the board with some slight increases.
I should like to refer to page 9 of this document, which is a public document tabled in the house, and ask that it be given consideration. On page 9 there is a detailed statement of the cost of improving the Lachine section for navigation alone. That is fixed at $87 million. On page 10 there is a detailed statement prepared by Quebec hydro of the cost of improving the Lachine section for power, and that amounts to $213 million. That makes a total of $300 million for the development of navigation and power in the Lachine section. Then there is another

Supply-Transport
detailed statement on page 10 showing the cost for a joint power and navigation development prepared by the officials of Quebec hydro in the amount of $266 million. Therefore anyone who looks at this report can see at once that there would be a saving of $34 million were the matter to be proceeded with jointly rather than separately, and these are the estimates prepared by the engineers of Quebec hydro. This is not only prepared by them but it covers a power development in the vicinity of Victoria bridge to the extent of 1,200,000 horsepower so that in accordance with the figures of Quebec hydro's own officials a joint development in 1948 would cost $34 million less than a separate one.
I should like to consider for a moment what transpired later. This is what happened. The then chairman of Quebec hydro and other officials thereof made their position clear to the officials of the St. Lawrence seaway authority. They stated that, speaking for themselves as private citizens and not as members of the hydroelectric power commission of Quebec and without having had any discussion with the premier of the province, they thought it would be extremely unwise to separate the development of the Lachine section into navigation and power. They thought that the development should be done jointly according to the plans prepared by the board of engineers in 1948 with which I have been dealing.
May I ask the hon. member from what document he was quoting?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am afraid the Solicitor General was not in the house when I gave that information. I am quoting from the 1948 report of the board of engineers.
What was the last document?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: So far as the last document is concerned, I have stated that the Quebec officials thought that the development should be done jointly according to the plan prepared by the board of engineers in 1948, with the modification that the canal should be on the south side rather than on the north side. Is there anything my hon. friend would like to ask?

I should like to make the record clear. You have quoted the chairman of the hydro commission as having made a certain statement independently, speaking personally, and not as chairman of the hydro commission. I am wondering what kind of document you are reading from.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I will tell my hon. friend what kind of document. If my hon. friend will take the trouble to go to the pertinent

department and consult the file he will find that everything contained in my speech is on the record.
Don't lose your temper.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I will do my best not to. He will find there that there is no doubt that all along the line the engineers of Quebec hydro felt that this should be a joint development rather than a separate development. So interested was Quebec hydro in the joint project that in 1951 it made a revision of the costs I have mentioned for a joint development in the Lachine section. This estimate amounted to $360 million without interest during construction, and that was made in October of 1951.
No further estimates were made by Quebec hydro as far as I am aware but the engineers of the Department of Transport made a further estimate on the basis of the price level in midsummer, 1953, and that estimate amounted to $400 million for the project which I have been discussing. The estimated cost of the construction of the canal for navigation alone in the Lachine section, adopting the location on the south shore, was approximately $125 million without interest during construction.
Still later, in May of 1954, the then chairman of the Quebec hydro commission-this is not just conjured up-made the suggestion that if an arrangement could be arrived at with the province of Quebec similar to that which was arrived at between the federal government and the province of Ontario in 1941 then his opinion was that he would be willing to recommend the joint development in the Lachine section if the federal government would do both works, the navigation works and the common works, and finance the whole project, Quebec hydro agreeing to pay back on the following basis, one-third in five years, one-third in ten years and one-third in fifteen years. That is not conjured up. That is a matter of record which my hon. friend can see if he will go to the trouble of looking at the files.
Then, in 1956 a commissioner of Quebec hydro announced in New York city that the Quebec government was going to develop power at Lachine and in January of 1959 a member of the Quebec government was reported to have made a similar announcement. Notwithstanding these two announcements, the province has not proceeded with the development.
However, it is well known that a firm of engineers has been appointed to study the problem and that plans for a two stage development, one at Heron island capable of developing 850,000 horsepower and the other

below the Victoria bridge, capable of developing 350,000 horsepower, have been prepared. These engineers have now been appointed for three years, and surely the public is entitled to know what their recommendations are, and what the plan is. After all, all of the engineering reports beginning with the international section and going right down to Lachine including Beauharnois, ever since they have been made from 1921 on, have been made public and submitted to this house. There is no reason why any other plans having to do with this matter should not be made public so that at least those of us who have an interest in it, the engineers who have an interest in it, could study them and give them consideration.
The question arises, why are they not produced? Why are they not made public? What is now envisaged clearly is a two stage development in that area. It may be possible to develop Lachine in two stages. Either one of these two stages might well cost the province less money if done separately, but they will cost the province more money if done together. What has always been envisaged is the development of 1,200,000 horsepower of electricity. It now looks as if the province is hedging on the development at Victoria bridge, alleging that frazil ice down the river is going to affect the potential. The question is rather this: Has the construction of the diversionary railway Victoria bridge precluded the province from a one stage scheme? The Canadian National Railways have now proceeded to construct that bridge on the assumption that there would not be a joint development of power and navigation in the vicinity of Victoria bridge. Proceeding with a one stage scheme might well mean the raising of two bridges instead of one, with a consequent loss of power below Victoria bridge amounting to 350,000 horsepower.
I come now to another matter which is germane to this discussion. It is the fact that the federal government made a substantial contribution toward the development of power in the international section. It is inconceivable to me that the federal government, if it had been asked to make an analogous contribution in the Lachine section or in the Beauharnois section, would not have made it. Now, what were those contributions? As the committee knows, the federal government did not proceed on the basis of the 1941 agreement upstream. This was discarded in the international section. It proceeded on another basis, that is that Ontario would pay for all the power facilities and the federal government would pay for all the navigational facilities, so that the old
Supply-Transport
division of 37i per cent navigation as opposed to 62J per cent power was discarded for the time being, each party paying its own costs.
Nevertheless, Canada agreed to contribute no less than $30 million for the development of power in the international section, $15 million before the work was started. There are some parts of that sum of money that are going to be voted during the consideration of the minister's estimates now. The federal government agreed to contribute $15 million toward the development of power in the international section. This was in lieu of so-called common works. Then, later on, when an impasse arose over the tailrace dredging to be done downstream in accordance with the order of approval of the I.J.C., dated October, 1952, there was a large amount of work that had to be done amounting to about $37 million, and of that the power entities agreed to pay $12 million leaving a balance of $25 million, $15 million of which was absorbed by Canada, again as assistance toward power development in the international section.
The point I make is this. It is inconceivable that the federal government would contribute $30 million toward power development upstream without being morally and equitably, if not legally, bound to contribute a similar amount downstream. By refusing to accept the advice of Quebec hydro, therefore, the government of Quebec lost an opportunity of a similar payment. Since the government of Quebec has, to all intents and purposes, decided to isolate itself in this, as in so many other matters, it would appear that a contribution of this magnitude may well be lost to the province forever. I think the house should know about this, as well as about a letter which was written by the late Mr. Mackenzie King, on March 12, 1941 to be exact, to the then premier of Quebec dealing with development in the Lachine section and in the Beauharnois section. He wrote saying, you have the right to develop power there jointly with us for navigation purposes, and we will do thus and so in the Beauharnois section and the Lachine section. I am quoting from page 71 of the correspondence and documents tabled in this house dealing with the great lakes-St. Lawrence basin development, 1938-1941:
With this end in view, the government of Canada would be prepared to undertake that, if and when Quebec takes over the control and operation of the Beauharnois development, there will be paid to the government of Quebec, by the government of Canada, the sum of $7,972,500.
This is nearly $8 million. As I have indicated before in this committee, that sum is worth far more now when you compare the

Supply-Transport
value of the dollar in 1959 with what it was then. I say, therefore, it is unfortunate that these sums which were legally undertaken by the federal government, were at least morally and equitably committed in these documents as well as in the contribution in the international section. I say that because the government of Quebec has lost a great opportunity to obtain a substantial payment toward two projects which are urgently required in the area.
I did want to speak about one or two other matters. I know that there are members here who want to speak, so I will not delay the committee. Perhaps I could conclude my remarks by thanking the minister for agreeing to table the correspondence with the hon. member for Peel, as he undertook to do earlier. I wonder whether he would not be good enough, while doing that, to let the committee have the minute of treasury board appointing the appraiser and which, I take it, defines his functions, and any other papers relating to his appointment and to his duties.

Still dealing with one matter affecting the St. Lawrence seaway, I was wondering whether the minister could give us an up to date report on the situation with regard to the relationship of the department or the seaway authority with the various contractors and their payments, especially their demands or requests for additional payments. I was most anxious to have an up to date report because the committee will recall that on March 9 the house authorized an order for return in the following words:
For a copy of all correspondence, telegrams, reports, briefs and other documents exchanged between the Minister of Transport or his deputies, and any official or agency of the government and any person, persons, or organizations, since December 1, 1958, dealing with claims made by contractors for payments from the St. Lawrence seaway authority.
As I say, Mr. Chairman, that order for return was passed in this house on March 9 and the department finally filed the return under sessional paper No. 165E on May 21. I will admit that it was quite a voluminous return and I have read it carefully. But I have one question I should like to ask the Minister of Transport. In view of the wording of the return, for all reports, briefs and other documents exchanged with any person, persons, or organizations since December 1, 1958, can he assure the committee that this sessional paper No. 165E fully conforms to the order of this house with regard to the filing of all documents?
I may say that I have been advised that it does not contain all the documents, especially a number which I had in mind

when I moved for the order for return. I know that there are certain individuals who seem to be persona non grata with the department as far as their names or their actions are concerned. I do not know the exact qualifications nor do I have a great deal of information about certain individuals, but I know that at approximately 11 o'clock this morning I was handed an affidavit. I was not going to put myself in the position of saying that certain papers which should have been filed had not been filed merely on the statement of an individual about whom I do not know a great deal. I felt that if that person wanted to put his information in the form of an affidavit, I myself would be protected when I make the statements I am now making. I am informed through the medium of this affidavit-
Order. Would the hon. member indicate whether he is going to ask the committee for permission to file the affidavit? Before he proceeds I should like to know that.
I will give all the information you want.

Is
the hon. member going to reveal the deponent of the affidavit?
It is an affidavit. I most certainly will do so.
Does he wish to file it?

Mr. Chairman, I shall be very glad to do so. With regard to the other matters of which the hon. member spoke, wherein he stated that certain material had been withheld from a return, may I say that I am not familiar with that matter although I certainly will have it checked up. If there is anything which should have been submitted and which was not submitted, I will certainly see that it is submitted. I would appreciate it greatly if the hon. member would give me the affidavit so that I can check the material to which he has referred.
Yes. I am filing the affidavit.
As to the situation in connection with claims at the present time, as of today claims have been received amounting to $38,959,957 on 30 contracts.

speechtext: I wonder if it would be possible to see that document? I should like to see it very much, because I have heard a great deal about this gentleman and I should like to read the affidavit. (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, at this stage of the consideration of the Department of

Supply-Transport
Transport's estimates, I should like to make a few remarks in order to draw the hon. minister's attention to certain problems affecting particularly the constituency I represent.
May I be allowed, first of all, to address very cordial thanks to the hon. minister who, since I have been member for Roberval, has always welcomed with much sympathy the representations I made to him on behalf of the citizens I represent.
I was listening a moment ago, with attention and at the same time with some amusement, to the remarks made by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) about the railway situation in the province of Quebec, and, in particular, about the Gaspe railway which was referred to by my colleague from Gaspe (Mr. English). He stated in particular that his party had not indulged in promises about railways. I readily understand that the hon. member for Laurier should say such things, since, having been absent from the province of Quebec for so many years, he is certainly not aware of what has been said in my constituency and in my district about the railways.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
On a point of order. I say that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) interrupted me earlier, it was not to deny that he had made promises in that constituency, but to ask me if the government had made promises during the 22 years we were in office. I replied that neither the government nor the minister of the day had made promises about the Gaspe railway, whereas the Prime Minister clearly did make promises in the statements he made out there.
The hon. member should not shift his ground; he may refer to the Prime Minister's statement, but he has no right to shift the subject.

Mr. Chairman, I admire the scruples of the hon. member for Laurier on that matter, but what I wanted to say was that the hon. member for Laurier is in a very weak position to talk about promises which have been made by the government, by the cabinet, by members or candidates, because my district and my constituency have heard so many Liberal promises about railways that only a stranger like the hon. member for Laurier, in my opinion, can refuse to admit that we have been deceived, and many times, about the railways. But that is not my point, Mr. Chairman. Besides, I do not pro-

pose to take too much stock in what the hon. member for Laurier has said.
What I want to emphasize once again in this house, is the urgent need for the Chi-coutimi-Lake St. John district that the railway line between Chicoutimi and Quebec be completely rebuilt. The rebuilding of that railway line is absolutely necessary. It is urgent today and that urgency takes on special character because of the industrial development which has taken place in our district and is still increasing.
Mr. Chairman, my colleague from Gaspe pointed out earlier that the province of Quebec has not been particularly favoured in the way of railroad construction. I think that remark applies even more aptly to the Chicoutimi-Lake St. John district and to my constituency, since for more than 25 years, all kinds of public organizations, bodies and municipalities have repeatedly asked for the rebuilding of this line between Chicoutimi and Quebec, and at a time when those representations should have been sympathetically received since a certain prosperity would have allowed the Canadian National Railways Company, at the time, to undertake the rebuilding of that Quebec-Chicoutimi line.
In fact, Mr. Chairman, it was in the years between 1939 and 1957 that the Canadian National Railway Company should have considered the building or the possibility of rebuilding that line, at a time when the economic situation was good, especially at a time when the requirements for railway transport were extremely great in our district. However it was not done, for despite all the representations that were made, despite all the pressures by public bodies, the government of the time and the Canadian National Railway Company ignored the repeated requests of the public men and of the population, in spite too of all the promises that were made successively in our district by Liberal members or candidates.
Mr. Chairman, I would point out to the hon. Minister of Transport that, as I indicated a moment ago, the industrial development now going on in my area as a result of its closeness to a mining centre, namely that of Chibougamau, makes the need for rebuilding this Chicoutimi-Quebec railway line a matter of even greater urgency. And here, Mr. Chairman, I am not raising a new fact. I need not even quote statistics, because the house has heard so many appeals, in the

last 20 or 25 years, from members from the province of Quebec. I refer in particular to the former independent member for Chicoutimi Mr. Paul Edmond Gagnon, to the hon. Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Balcer), and to members who, every year, pointed out to the house the problem of rebuilding the Chicoutimi-Quebec railway.
The present situation is deplorable. Please note, Mr. Chairman, that it is not my intention to lay a charge against the Canadian National. I simply wish to set the facts again in their proper light. The railway line from Chicoutimi to Quebec, including the section serving the Lake St. John area, is inadequate, does not meet present requirements of modern transportation, and does not meet the requirements of industrial development that has taken place in our area.
Mr. Chairman, this railway line from Chicoutimi to Quebec, which includes a section from Chambord to Dolbeau, and another as far as Alma, could also be extended so as to circle Lake St. John, because it is not normal, in our modern times, that a railway should not serve all the people of an area such as ours.
That request was possibly made in the past. I refer to it now, however, because a railway line circling the whole of lake Saint John, it seems to me, would be of great advantage to the citizens of my constituency as well as to those of adjoining constituencies. While it might not be possible for obvious reasons at the present time to carry out that project, it is one that must be considered. Those suggestions should also be considered because they are in the best interest of an expanding area whose development is bound to be even greater in years to come.
Mr. Chairman, this matter of the rebuilding of the Chicoutimi-Quebec railway must not however throw into the background other projects such as for instance, the one my hon. colleague from Chicoutimi (Mr. Brassard) has in mind, namely the construction of a railway into northern Quebec.
The other day again, I listened with much amusement and interest to the remarks made in this connection by the hon. member for Laurier. I found this former minister of transport had a remarkable solicitude for our area, a solicitude which has not always been his, of course, especially when you remember the circumstances which surrounded the construction of the Chibougamau-St. Felicien railway.

My second matter, Mr. Chairman-

Neither of these shops is in my constituency, but the people who are affected by those lay-offs do reside in my constituency. I have received some representations. The news reports of those proposed lay-offs have been conflicting, to say the least. There have been a number of conflicting reasons advanced for those layoffs. Mr. Chairman, with regard to the last question, I am afraid I am not familiar with this particular case because it is something that comes under the management of the Canadian National Railways. Mr. Chairman, 1 should like to speak briefly about a number of matters which interest my district considerably. As the constituency of Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador stretches from the airport at Gander north to the airport at Goose and then on to cape Chidley in the far north, naturally transportation and communications are of paramount importance to us. I have in mind particularly communications along the Labrador coast. In many small places the only means of communication are small radiotelephone sets. They serve a very good purpose in so far as they are available but there are altogether too few of them. Particularly during the winter time, when practically all transportation ceases except by air, the radiotelephone set is the only means of communication with the outside, the only means by which a doctor can be summoned or other messages sent in time of need.
As I have pointed out to the department on a number of occasions, more of these radiotelephone sets are required. I am told that the situation today is not as good as it was some years ago and in this connection I should like to read from a report prepared by Mr. George Sellars, M.H.A., the provincial member for Labrador South. He says:
Before wireless telegraphy became established, Canada supported a telegraph line along the Quebec north shore which extended to Red Bay. When a wireless was opened at Belle isle for communicating with steamers operating via the straits of Belle isle route a station was also established at Chateau, Point Amour, Point Riche, Newfoundland and Grindstone island and on up the St. Lawrence river. As improvements were made the stations at Chateau and also at Point Riche, Newfoundland, were closed and Belle isle worked Point Amour and Point Amour worked direct with Grindstone. Subsequently, Belle isle has been working Grindstone direct so that Point Amour is now working mostly as a radio beacon.
In the early days there were several wireless stations established in eastern Labrador chief among them being Battle Harbour which in the early days of wireless communicated with Fogo and Fogo communicated with St. John's by land line. Later Battle Harbour communicated with St. John's (Signal Hill) direct and Fogo station closed. Along Labrador there were wireless stations located at the following places, viz: Fishing Ships Harbour,

Venison Island, Hawkes Harbour, Domino, Flat Island, Grady, Smokey, Halton, Makkovik, Hope-dale, Cartwright, Cape Harrison.
Today the situation is: Battle Harbour, due to close this summer and to be replaced by a telephone; Marys Harbour, radiophone operated by Grenfell mission and used for communication with St. Anthony; Port Hope Simpson, logging centre, 25 miles up Alexis river or bay; Fishing Ships Harbour, private-Fishery Products-out in winter; Snug Harbour, private-Fishery Products-operates June to October; Hawkes Harbour, private-whaling company-now closed; Square Islands, private- B.W. Powell; Frenchman's Island, Department of Transport; Black Tickle, Department of Transport; Cartwright, Department of Transport; Parks Harbour, private, S. B. Fequet and Son.
Two large settlements in Sandwich bay and widely separated, Paradise and Separation Point, should have radiophones as should other settlements, particularly Paradise, Separation Point, Spotted Island, Batteau, Hawkes Harbour, George's Cove, Williams Harbour, Fox Harbour, Cape Charles, Marys Harbour.
The Minister of Transport suggested people of Spotted Island should form co-op and purchase radiophone and operate it without cost to D.O.T. after getting a $10 licence from Moncton.
Marys Harbour cannot handle commercial correspondence. There is only one nurse there and her time is fully occupied and it is very unreasonable to ask her to handle communications.
The decision to have Labrador traffic routed via Cartwright and Goose presents almost insurmountable difficulties. The high Mealy mountains are directly between Cartwright and Goose and in my experience these mountains are the birthplace and habitation of every known kind of atmosphere disturbance and static, so much so that it cannot be relied on for a constant communications channel.
Besides the cost of sending a telegram from Newfoundland to Labrador was until lately 55 cents. What will it cost via the maritimes and Quebec to Goose and Cartwright to destination in Labrador? The government of Canada ought to provide us with the same land line service that it provides over the same line for Quebec. Our portion of the line has not been repaired while the portion through Quebec is kept in A-l condition. Why should they let our portion of the line go into decay?
That was written by the provincial member for Labrador South. The point I am trying to make is that improved communications are needed along the Labrador coast. These communications form the only means by which the people of these isolated places can keep in contact with the outside world in order to make their needs known and obtain medical aid when it is required. As was stated in the letter, some of the sets are privately owned, some are owned by the Grenfell mission which operates on that coast and a number of places have no means of communication whatsoever.
Another matter of vital interest to Labrador and northern Newfoundland is air strips. Last year the Newfoundland department of highways built an air strip at Nain on the Labrador coast, helped to complete one at North West River, the seat of the Grenfell mission in Labrador, and
Supply-Transport
began one at St. Anthony, the headquarters of the international Grenfell association. The one at Nain is being used. I believe the one at North West River is being used but needs to be extended. The one at St. Anthony needs to be completed.' In addition, another air strip is badly required at Cartwright in Labrador while Baie Verte, Roddickton and Port Saunders are centres in northern Newfoundland that should be considered, as also should La Scie, although I understand that it will probably be difficult to get a suitable location at La Scie. I might also mention Hopedale in northern Labrador.
I hope that the minister will be able to do something about the construction of these air strips or some of them during this season. Large air strips are not needed. Small gravel strips on which Beaver aircraft can land are sufficient in most places, although it might be desirable to extend the runways at North West River and St. Anthony to take larger aircraft. Basically what is required are gravel or dirt strips on which Beavers can operate. They would be used largely by the planes supplied to the Grenfell mission by the Newfoundland government. These planes are used extensively for servicing the coast and to bring in patients to the Grenfell mission hospitals. I might add that at Nain eleven people died two years ago because a plane could not land there with serum.
The Newfoundland government built a small airstrip at Nain last year. As I mentioned, the value of this airstrip is particularly high during the periods of freeze-up and breakup. During the summer the planes can operate on floats, and during the winter they can operate on skis. However, during the periods of freeze-up in the fall and breakup in the spring they can use neither skis nor floats and strategically located airstrips are essential so that air services can be carried out during the whole 12 months.
I should like to mention a word or two here about Goose Bay. During Easter I was fortunate enough to be able to visit Goose Bay. While there I saw, to some extent, the preparations for defence, the superb communications, and sensed to some degree at least the global thinking of the warriors who were there. Suddenly the world seemed very small and Canada seemed a lot safer. I should like to pay tribute to those who operate this great airfield and those who are in command. I should like to mention in particular Mr. James Murphy, the head of D.O.T. at Goose Airport, Group Captain W. Swetman, Officer Commanding the R.C.AF. Station, Col. A. J. Beck, Wing Commander, U.S.A.F., Magistrate Terry J. Corbett and

Sergt. Pat Byers R.C.M.P. There exists among them a high degree of working co-operation which is equalled by the efficiency.
Now, I should like to say a word about Gander, where a native Newfoundlander, Mr. Rex Tilley is doing a fine job for the Department of Transport. A hotel is badly needed at Gander because I understand that passengers show little enthusiasm for spending the night there. A large modern terminal will soon be opened by her Majesty the Queen, something of which we are all proud. This, in itself, is a source of gratification to everybody, not only those who are interested in Gander but those who are interested in Canada because Gander is the only part of Canada which many people see. People going through from one continent to another often pause at Gander, and I think it is only proper that a fine terminal should be there as a monument to Canada because Gander is the real gateway to Canada. Gander is the first part of Canada that many people see coming from the other side. As I say, a hotel is really needed. Often planes have to remain there overnight and the accommodation at the present time is poor.
A suggestion has been made that Gander should be a free port. The flying public, I understand, prefers to make stops at places where the facilities of a free port exist. Recently there has been a tendency to by-pass Gander, particularly with the development of large, long range aircraft. I would suggest that nothing be overlooked which would make it attractive for people to stop at Gander. Then, the pressure from passengers may influence the airlines to make Gander an extra stop. I will add, too, that some of the pilots seem to be objecting to regulations respecting vaccination, etc., and I hope the Minister of Transport will speak to his colleague the minister of health to see if there cannot be some relaxation of these regulations commensurate with safety.
No word about Gander would be complete without a word of praise for Eastern Provincial Airways. They have an unexcelled record for safety and service. This company has flown many miles since its inception and its safety record is excellent and the stories of the mercy flights undertaken are legion. They perform a very vital part in the communications in Newfoundland, particularly in the more remote parts of the province. I do not believe any word about Eastern Provincial Airways would be complete without mentioning its general manager, Mr. A. J. Lew-ington, its traffic manager, Mr. Marsh Jones and its maintenance manager, Mr. William Harris.

The minister would probably expect that a member from Prince Edward Island would have a word to say about transportation. I am sure that all his predecessors down through the years have known that this is one subject that is dear to us in Prince Edward Island. With my usual laconic brevity I should like to mention one or two aspects of the activities of this department.
I will not speak at length about the car ferries because the minister has heard much about it from myself and my colleagues for a long time. However, I would say that it is of the utmost importance that speed be of the essence in the construction of a new ferry in this area and in the interim I would urge on the minister that every measure be taken to make full and maximum use of existing facilities. The planking of the Scotia II is an important step but I wish he would, with the C.N.R., look into the prospects of making more trips with the existing ferries when the traffic demands it. I am convinced that there could be more and later trips which would help move cars and a great number of people wanting-and wisely so-to go to Prince Edward Island. This main transportation link is one which connects with the railway because that was a vital term of our confederation agreement that we were to be kept in continuous and efficient communication with the mainland. In that aspect there is an important consideration, namely that we have a speedier rail service from Moncton down to Cape Tormentine. It takes an interminable time to make that short trip which ties in with the major transportation link. That would be a vast improvement. I know the minister is convinced of the importance of that matter.

If I might just answer the question of the hon. member in order to show how quickly we accede to requests in this department. I am pleased to tell him that officials of the Department of Transport, the C.N.R. and the Department of Public Works are at Borden and Tormentine today doing just what he has in mind, namely improving transportation facilities, as he has so correctly outlined in his speech.

In order to show my deep appreciation I think the best thing I can do is to move immediately from that subject, say a word or two on one more matter and then resume my seat. For a long time we have been interested in improving the airport in Charlottetown so that it might have a runway which would allow for the landing of larger aircraft. I am happy that work is progressing there on the building of a 66968-9-289

7,000-foot runway. I think that will make a great improvement in the transportation picture in our province and, of course, in the whole Atlantic area. The hon. member who has just spoken mentioned the airport facilities in Winnipeg. I may say that in that regard Charlottetown is ahead of Winnipeg. For that I should like to say that the minister's energetic and swift action is much commended.

Mr. Chairman, although there are several interesting matters which I might usefully discuss on the estimates of the Minister of Transport, I have chosen to say a relatively few words on a project which is not new to the committee nor to the house but which I think is a timely one to be brought back before the committee at this time. I noticed a while ago just how quick the Minister of Transport was in answering requests from hon. members. I sincerely hope that the request that I shall make will receive the same quick action that we saw just a few moments ago.
I propose to say a few words about the Richelieu waterway or the Champlain waterway as some prefer to call it. As hon. members know, for many years there has been some traffic along the Richelieu river across lake Champlain and down the Hudson river to New York. Because of the nature of the waters it has not been possible for any ships of any size to go through this canal. But ever since the turn of the century representations have continually been made to the government asking it to create a navigable waterway from the St. Lawrence to the city of New York on this particular route. As the years went on and the recommendations and representations were more and more numerous the government decided to have the international joint commission study the project. In 1937 the international joint commission made some recommendations which I think would be useful if they were put on Hansard. At page 17 of the interim report of the international joint commission on the Champlain waterway we read as follows:
Taking into consideration the fact already mentioned that neither the engineers nor any of the interested parties who appeared before the commission in support of or in opposition to the proposed waterway, were of the opinion that it could be justified, if at all, except as an extension of or in connection with the St. Lawrence deep waterway and the fact that the St. Lawrence waterway is not yet assured and in any event could not be completed and put into operation for a number of years; and the further fact that it is impossible to foresee the changes that may take place in transportation in the meantime, or to estimate the

Supply-Transport
bearing the completion of the St. Lawrence waterway might have on the advisability of constructing the improvement now under consideration,-
And this part is important.
-the commission recommends that the present report be considered an interim report, and that it be authorized to retain jurisdiction over the matter until the St. Lawrence waterway has become an accomplished fact and the commission has had an opportunity of studying the effect of its operation upon the proposed Champlain waterway.
Of course this recommendation of the international joint commission at that time put a wet blanket on the project of the Champlain waterway. But once the St. Lawrence seaway had been decided upon, and more particularly as it approached its completion, there were increased activity and increased interest on the part of officials, municipal and civic, both in Canada and in the United States. Over the past few years I remember how many meetings were held either in Sorel or in Plattsburg with officials both of municipalities along the Richelieu river and those in the United States. Chambers of commerce had made repeated representations to the government and many other civic organizations have made similar representation.
Just about a year ago a United States-Canada delegation presented a rather complete and thorough brief to the Prime Minister. According to the Prime Minister's statement, it would appear that he was greatly interested in and taken up with the project. As a result, he promised that he would come to the area in Sorel and travel on the Richelieu river in order to see the project at first hand. Unfortunately-and I can well imagine that it was unavoidable-he was not able to carry out that particular promise. On this occasion I should like to extend to the Prime Minister a further invitation to come to Sorel at which time we will make it amply possible for him to visit what I think is a natural project and one which would be a most useful economical project.
On the United States side there has been as much if not more interest in this particular project. I could cite I do not know how many newspapers on the activities that have taken place in the United States and the comments that have been made on this project. But I think perhaps the greatest evidence of interest in the United States would be given if I quote an article that appeared in La Presse on April 28, 1959:
(Translation):
Consideration is given to a canal connecting Sorel to New York.
Washington, 28, (PCF)-A submission was made yesterday to the American congress for a $10,000 appropriation to allow for continuation of a preliminary study of a proposed canal connecting New York to the St. Lawrence. The present waterway through the Hudson river and lake Champlain provides a channel which is 12 feet deep on the

United States side, but shallower in Canada, in the Richelieu river.
(Text):
I believe it is quite evident that the United States has this project very much at heart and that we in Canada should see to it that a similar study is made. I am not sure whether it will be necessary, as written in the interim report of the international joint committee, to set up another body to conduct the study or whether, as stated on page 17 of the report, the present report could be considered an interim report and that it be authorized to retain jurisdiction on the matter. I am not sure whether or not the international joint commission would automatically go into this study or not but I should like to have the minister assure the committee that a study will be made at this time for the realization of a project which, to me, is an important Canadian project.
I think it would be useful at this time to read into the record the conclusions which were arrived at by the international commission. I quote from page 15 of the report:
Directing itself therefore, to the questions: Is it advisable to improve a waterway from Montreal through lake Champlain to connect with the Hudson river; and what is the estimated cost of such a waterway; the commission finds:
(1)	That there are five possible routes for a waterway from Montreal to the Hudson river by way of lake Champlain, the last-mentioned being an allwater route and the remainder overland routes, as follows:
(a)	From lake St. Francis on the St. Lawrence river to lake Champlain via the Chazy river.
(b)	From lake St. Francis to the Richelieu river three miles south of the city of St. Johns.
(c)	From Caughnawaga, on the St. Lawrence river, to Fryer's island on the Richelieu river.
(d)	From the St. Lawrence at Longueuil to Fryer's island on the Richelieu river.
(e)	From the St. Lawrence river at Sorel up the Richelieu river to lake Champlain.
I should like to draw the attention of the committee, in particular to what follows. I continue the quotation:
In the case of all five routes the existing waterway would be followed through lake Champlain and by way of the Champlain canal to the Hudson river at Albany.
(2)	That of these five routes, the last-mentioned (e) is the most practicable from an engineering standpoint and the least impracticable from an economic point of view.
I think I should remind the committee that this report was written in 1937, and that the development which has taken place in that area since has confirmed to my mind that from an engineering standpoint it would be far more favourable than any of the other alternatives and that from an economic standpoint it would be of the greatest advantage to all concerned. We recall that according to the first plans the St. Lawrence seaway canal was supposed to run on the Montreal

side of the river, but for some reason or another the plan was changed subsequently and the canal now runs on the south shore of the St. Lawrence. If any of the other alternatives were adopted it would mean that the Richelieu waterway would have to cut through the St. Lawrence seaway. It seems to me that there is already sufficient bottling-up around the St. Lawrence seaway without causing additional hazards in that area.
The other reason is that the channel of the Richelieu river, like that of the Hudson river, can only be a maximum of 12 feet. Because of the narrowness of both rivers, if the draught of the river were to be lower than 12 feet it would cost a fortune to sustain the river banks along both these routes. As a matter of fact, also, in favour of the natural water route, in 1937 there was some preparatory work done on the Richelieu river and a considerable amount of money was spent. The dam at St. Ours was reconstructed to take navigation at 12 feet. The Fryer's island dam was also built in prevision of the Richelieu waterway from lake Champlain right down to Sorel, and as a matter of fact the greater part of the Richelieu river as it is now is already 12 feet and it would to my mind cost very little to make it 12 feet all the way.
From an economic standpoint it seems to me that most of the ships which would be using the Richelieu waterway would come from below Montreal and below Sorel. They would be ships transporting paper and iron ore and would normally come up the St. Lawrence to turn into the Richelieu at Sorel. I think very little shipping would be made directly from Montreal to use this water route. Also in past years there has been a considerable evolution in the industrialization of the south shore and it would appear that within a relatively short number of years there will be several steel industries located there. All these industries would be greatly assisted if freight could move via the Richelieu river and on to New York rather than going up to Montreal and having to wait in order to get into the St. Lawrence seaway canal and from there having to enter into another canal and cross territory in order to reach the Richelieu river at St. Johns. I think it would be a serious mistake to divert ships in this way. I think it would be unprofitable to the companies to which I have referred and I think it would be endangering the seaway by cluttering it up with more ships than it has already. It seems to me that the seaway has enough trouble as it is without causing any further inconvenience.
So I make the suggestion to the minister and say that the time is now ripe for a study to be made of the project. I personally feel 66968-9-289J
Supply-Transport
that the most logical, most economic and best route would be to follow the natural route of the river from St. Johns to Sorel. I think it would be less costly and would prove far more effective than any other means.
I sincerely hope that the minister will look into this matter very seriously and if it is at all possible for him to do so to have either the international joint commission or some other body study the possibilities of this project. I invite the minister along with the Prime Minister to visit this area. We would be happy indeed to travel along the Richelieu river with them to follow the route which we believe to be the most desirable and in the best interests.

Mr. Chairman, normally when an hon. member rises in committee or in the house with a pile of books or documents on his desk it is sometimes indicative of rather extensive notes but far be it from me to involve myself in the problem of reading speeches.
In respect of some issues and particularly one now current in my constituency I receive letters and in this instance I suggest that by comparison Perry Como is a bit of a piker. The letters and documents in the folders on my desk refer to a matter which I am sure is well known to the minister. It concerns the Canadian National Railways by-pass over the north end of Toronto. The greater part of the proposed route to be followed falls within the boundaries of the constituency of York-Scarborough.
Perhaps before putting a specific question to the minister I should give the committee some background concerning this matter. The original proposal for this proposed bypass and the route it was to follow was put forward by the Canadian National Railways some time ago. It was greeted with mixed feelings in various areas and it is not surprising that many individuals owning and occupying homes in or near the proposed route of the by-pass were most upset and concerned. Judging from the many letters I have received on this subject and as a result of my personal observations in the constituency over the proposed route there is not on the part of the people concerned any specific argument or disagreement as to the necessity for the by-pass itself. The economic benefits that will flow into the area and into metropolitan Toronto in general are conceded to be valid in every respect.
There have been a number of ratepayer groups formed in various sections of my constituency and neighbouring constituencies involved in this matter. When the original route proposal was announced maps were made available to residents in the area. Various groups were formed, some of them outgrowths of existing ratepayer groups, and some special groups were organized to look into the matter with a view to making recommendations in respect of this proposed route.
I must say that the officials of the Canadian National Railways and the minister have been most co-operative in acceding to my demands that every reasonable consideration should be given to persons who are likely

to be affected by this route and in the main that pledge and undertaking has been met.
More recently a group of ratepayers was formed in the Thornhill area comprising some engineers qualified to examine and assess various aspects of engineering data which I quite freely confess are beyond my grasp. This committee met on many occasions and expended a great deal of time, effort and money in examining an alternative route which was then proposed to the C.N.R. based on the general conditions set down in the original announcement. This alternative route would largely by-pass the village of Thornhill, move northward along existing C.N.R. lines and would cross Yonge street at a point which in the view of the committee would affect fewer people. This route in the view of the committee would be consistent with the original undertaking given by the Canadian National Railways.
The alternative route proposal was studied by the engineering division of the railway and within the last week the project director of the railway company wrote to the people concerned in the following terms:
A detailed study of the second route was undertaken and, on completion of our studies, we expressed the view that this route failed to compare favourable with the one originally chosen by us.
Since the last meeting with your committee of engineers, we have again studied the second route and have confirmed our decision that there are no compelling characteristics to this route over that originally selected by the Canadian National Railways-
I would like to repeat, Mr. Chairman, I am not qualified to judge the relative engineering merits of these two alternate routes but I would appreciate some comment from the minister concerning this when I resume my seat. This group having advanced specific reasons of a humane nature concerning the possible effect on schools, school children, the health of the residents in the Thornhill area; having examined this question in a manner and to a degree that certainly surprised me; having dealt with such matters as degrees of sound emitted by diesel engines, the amount of dust, and so on, suspended in the air, and many other related factors; having done this, having conducted a count of the adjacent homes affected by this original proposed route and, as I say, having obtained more engineering data, they received what in their view and in their opinion, as a result of the letters I have received this week, amounted to an out of hand refusal. I certainly feel that if there are good and sufficient reasons why this original route must prevail we are all prepared to adopt a reasonable attitude in this regard. I would respectfully submit, Mr. Chairman, that this group is entitled to a point by point rebuttal of the
Supply-Transport
proposals they have put forward and an answer to the reasons they have advanced in support of their case.
I do not wish to detain the committee. I am ready to resume my seat and ask the minister whether he would submit to my specific demand for a further review of this matter and certainly a more specific and detailed rebuttal of the proposals put forward by this group.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, I shall be very glad to accede to the hon. member's request. If he will give me the correspondence to which he has referred I shall be glad to forward it to the management of the Canadian National Railways and request that this matter be given fuller consideration and a full and detailed answer given to the people on whose behalf the hon. member has just spoken.
While I am on my feet I should like to answer questions put to me earlier by the hon. member for Assiniboia. He complained about certain work on the locks of the St. Lawrence seaway which, in his judgment, had not been properly finished. I have spoken to the president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority and he has given me the following report: The hon. member referred to the construction work which, according to his information or judgment, did not appear to be satisfactory. In a work so complicated and extensive as the seaway, with a good deal of winter construction, there are likely to be individual items of work which in the first instance do not meet the specifications. It is the responsibility of the engineering staff to insist upon remedial measures and satisfactory work, failing which there are retained funds to protect the public interests. I am assured that this course has been followed in seaway construction and that where work remains to be done sufficient funds to cover the same are held back.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few brief remarks on the transportation estimates, as transportation has always been one of our most important problems. Recently we have seen considerable progress made in solving some of those problems. First, there was the reduction in the freight rates and more recently the announcement of a new car ferry which will be designed to meet our specific needs in carrying the increased car and truck traffic across the Northumberland strait. The announcement was very well received and the people of our province are grateful to the Minister of Transport for the consideration he has given the province.
An effort was made to stampede the federal government into purchasing a second-hand

Mr. Chairman, before the first item is passed I should like to make a few remarks with regard to the transportation problems concerning our province and particularly my own constituency of Kings. I hope the committee will not be bored with the repetition of our island problems but I know it is appreciated that because of our insular position we are very "transportation conscious" and all our people are very sensitive to our problems in that regard.
Last week I spent a few days in my constituency visiting the very many fishing harbours all along the coast. I should like to say a few words about navigational lights. Our larger harbours have been pretty well taken care of for a number of years but unfortunately the smaller ones have been more or less neglected. I want to commend the government on the installation of the new small lights of the Wallace and Tiernan type, which are being installed in a great many of our harbours and which have proven very successful besides being very economical to instal and maintain. I should like to commend them also for the rebuilding of lightkeepers' accommodations. When I visited Souris I found, not very far from the splendid federal building which is being erected, that the foundation had been completed for a new lightkeepers' dwelling in that area. This is the second one replaced under this government.
In the waters off the eastern part of Prince Edward Island we have a great abundance of fish which has attracted a great many draggers during the past few years. Representations have been made by the dragger owners' association for the erection of a ship to shore telephone service at East point. There is a small one operated by a private company at Souris but it is

not nearly adequate to look after the problems that the draggermen have when at sea. We all realize that this is a very dangerous occupation and a very monotonous one at times, and there is a great lack of adequate communication with the mainland. The only suitable place for the erection of such a station is at East point and I would strongly urge the minister to give early consideration to the problem of the dragger fishermen in that area.
We in the maritimes have been very interested to note that the icebreaker facilities of the department have been enlarged this year. I want to thank the minister for providing assistance to the sealing industry during the past two winters. On several occasions icebreakers of the department provided assistance at a critical time and it was greatly appreciated by those engaged in that industry. Now that these icebreakers are in operation I should like to mention that prime consideration should be given to the ports of Souris and Georgetown in my constituency which are the latest to remain open in the province. I might say that sometimes at the tail end of the season the whole province depends on the use of these two ports for the export of large shipments of potatoes, particularly to southern United States markets, and it is very important that we have good icebreaking service. We have been fairly successful to date and I hope that with the new facilities available we will have no difficulties whatsoever in that regard.
In passing may I say with regard to icebreaking on the St. Lawrence that I believe there is a limit to what we can do in bucking nature. I know that during the last season winter set in more quickly and severely than had been expected, but I do not think so much expense is warranted in any year to try to keep the St. Lawrence open.
I should also like to submit that a landing strip should be constructed in Kings county. I may say that this was recommended to the royal commission on transportation, often known as the "Turgeon Commission", and we feel that we are at a considerable disadvantage economically in our county because of the fact that we have never had an air strip there. There are many advantages economically and otherwise which would follow the construction of such an air strip and I hope the department will give strong consideration to this in the near future.
One of our main problems with regard to transportation, of course, is the connection with the mainland. As has been said over and over again, one of the terms under which we entered confederation was that we would be provided with "continuous and adequate
Supply-Transport
transportation to the mainland", and ever since there have been a great many problems involved in maintaining that link. I am not going to go into the whole history because it is very lengthy and has been given on very many occasions.
We know that the present service is by large icebreaking ferries which carry railway cars, and it has been considered for a number of years that this service is not sufficient. Various other solutions have been discussed, for example, the building of a tunnel or a bridge and latterly the building of a causeway. I might say that the last suggestion is perhaps the most practical and economical. The previous government talked about the construction of a causeway for some years but I know they did not do a great deal about it because I have a letter in my office from the Department of Public Works stating that they spent only $6,600 in investigating the possibility of building such a causeway. That is insignificant in comparison with the over $600,000 which has been spent or appropriated to be spent on a thorough survey to determine whether or not a causeway is feasible.
There are, of course, many factors to be considered such as: tides, ice conditions, the effect on fisheries, the availability of fill near the point of construction and armour rock for the sides of the causeway, whether a railway track will be included in the project, and so on. However, we are still hopeful that the project will be declared feasible and we are awaiting with interest the final report on the causeway survey. Even if it is declared feasible, of course, it would be a project which would take a number of years to complete. Meanwhile, the traffic to and from Prince Edward Island continues to grow. We appreciate very much the recent action taken to help the situation by the appropriation for a new boat at the earliest possible time. We feel that the construction of a new boat and the expansion of all the available facilities, such as the minister mentioned were being investigated, will be of great assistance in alleviating our transportation problems. I can assure the minister this is greatly appreciated by the people of Prince Edward Island.
I have a rather long range request. I should like to suggest that if the causeway becomes a reality and some of these boats are available, a new service might be inaugurated between Pictou and Georgetown, P.E.I. Both of these points have splendid harbours, and we have no hesitation in saying that we feel the service will be very popular and very well patronized. In summing up, Mr. Chairman, I would just ask the minister and his departmental officials to

Supply-Transport
give urgent and early consideration to three points I mentioned, namely: the ship to shore station at East point; the expansion of the icebreaking service next fall, and the construction of a landing strip in Kings county.

I have been most uncomfortable this afternoon, Mr. Chairman. I have perspired, occasionally retired, and now I feel like expiring. I have been looking around for the reason and suddenly my eyes fell on the calendar, June 10. It was on a former June 10 in 1957 that there was a political volcano erupted in Canada and, unfortunately from our point of view, a lot of Conservative lava flowed over some jolly good C.C.F. members. We are working hard during these months, and we expect they will come to life again before the next election.
I am going to make a few very brief remarks on this item. I have a few other remarks to make on the particular items, but I like to deal with particular matters under the particular items so that the minister has the appropriate officials in front of him, although I know the deputy minister is familiar with most of these matters.
For a number of years I have raised my voice in this house on behalf of the people in the southeastern portion of British Columbia in protest against the inadequate service on the Kettle Valley railway. I want at this time to thank the minister for the part he has played in making arrangements with the board of transport commissioners to hold public hearings in Nelson on June 22. I can say, Mr. Chairman that there has been an excellent response to that opportunity by the people in the southern interior of British Columbia. They will let the board of transport commissioners know what they think about the present service. I can assure the minister and the board there will be strong representations from chambers of commerce, from trade unions and from other bodies who, when they make their representations before the board, will speak for all the people in the southern interior of British Columbia, regardless of party.
I just want to take this opportunity to bring a matter to the attention of the committee, and it entered my mind because I have been dealing for a few minutes with the curtailment of service and the inadequate service on the Kettle Valley railroad. It was brought to my attention by a very old gentleman in my riding who has had a lot of experience throughout the years in northern Canada, and who has made a very close study of the railroad needs of the country. I promised him to bring this matter before the house. While doing this, I want to say that

I remember, in conversation with him, reading the minutes of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines or possibly the committee on government railways, I am not sure-I am getting on in years and my memory fails me on occasion-where there was a reference to the thousands of miles of railroad owned by the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific in the United States, while we in Canada are suffering a curtailment of passenger service in various places and the abandonment of passenger service in other places.
It is my opinion, Mr. Chairman, that not only should we make a study of freight rates and the cost of freight rates to the carrying on of business in this country, but I think there should be some study given by the government and its agencies to the level of passenger service required to meet the needs of the people of Canada. I think there should be some study made and some co-ordination of the present services. There should be some study of the necessity for building railroads to meet the needs of the future. I think we should begin to look at this question now, and the proper authority to give the lead on that question is the government of Canada and particularly the Minister of Transport. I make that suggestion, and when the minister replies I should like to get his comments. I do not make that as a suggestion-
I wonder if I could ask the hon. gentleman a question?
Certainly.
Does he not think it was the action of his neighbours, the Doukhobors, that caused the curtailment of passenger service and the higher freight rates in that area?

Nothing of the sort; the Canadian Pacific Railway took advantage of the situation created by a few indecent bombs to curtail the service as quickly as possible; that is the opinion in my district. Anyone can prove that by the fact that there are freight trains running 24 hours a day, while the passenger trains are running in the daylight. All the bridges have lights and there are handcars to proceed over the bridge first to make sure it is safe. If the needs of the people are considered by the persons concerned, if the board of transport commissioners and the officials of the Canadian Pacific railway get together, I am sure they will be able to work out something that will be satisfactory to all concerned, especially if they enter these negotiations in the right spirit and with good will.

I mentioned this need for a study particularly of the railroad requirements of Canada with respect to passenger service, the existing railroads and the need for extension of them.
Before concluding, I want to bring the minister's attention to a map which has been supplied me by this very old gentleman who has studied the problem for years. I promised him I would bring this up in the house. He suggests there is an opportunity in the future for a third national railway to serve the more northerly portion of Canada. I see the minister opening his mouth and looking with despair, but I said an opportunity in the future. According to this gentleman's map, there is an opportunity in the future for a third national railway to serve the northern portion of Canada by connecting up a lot of railways that exist today. His plan here shows the railway starting at Winnipeg, going to Hudson Bay Junction, Birch Hills, Meadow Lake, Boyle, Athabasca, McLennan, Hines Creek, and eventually to Prince Rupert.
I just told this gentleman I would bring his suggestion before the committee. He has been very keen about it. I think he has written some letters to former ministers of transport throughout the years, and possibly to some officials in the department. In making these few remarks, I am keeping my word to this old gentleman. When a person takes the time to buy books, travel at his own expense and study a problem, even though his solution may not be the correct one, I think it is the proper attitude on the part of anyone in public life to do anything they can to recognize that spirit. This old gentleman, who is nearly 90, is still interested in the development of Canada. I wish there were a good many young people between the ages of 15 and 20 who were as interested in the development of this country at this time as this old gentleman. I bring that matter to the attention of the minister and I should like to have his comments when he replies at a later date.

I should be very glad to look over that study and the recommendations which the hon. member has just mentioned. It sounded extremely interesting. If he would be good enough to let me have it, I and my officials will be glad to give it careful study.

speechtext:
I should like to join with my colleague the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres in dealing with a matter which is of extreme importance not only to himself but to all Quebec members, particularly those in the Montreal area. I refer, of course, to the Champlain cut-off or the Richelieu waterway as it is often called. It is a question which has been under discussion for some years. It is one with which the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres is more conversant than am I. It is one that should be engaging the attention of the House of Commons at this time.
I say that, Mr. Chairman, not only because of the representations which have been made to many hon. members, and more particularly to hon. members opposite, but also to several of the ministers of the present government. I know that groups and associations have banded themselves together in order to make the requisite recommendations in favour of this waterway. I think the time has arrived, first, for the appointment of a board of engineers to consider the economics of this waterway. I do not suggest that the time has arrived to go beyond that point yet. But in order to have a perfect understanding of the problem that is before us there must be at least some sort of economic or engineering study; and that is what I want to plead for on this occasion.
The committee knows the matter engaged the attention of the international joint commission many years ago. The matter came before the international joint commission because it concerned, I presume, boundary waters; it concerned waters which had to do with the Richelieu river and the canals of Canada, including the Champlain and St. Ours canals, as well as the Champlain waterway together with the Hudson river. Because of the fact that several states of the union were interested in the project, the matter was referred to the international joint commission for determination. That was done back in 1937.
The international joint commission at that time considered a number of alternate routes. It is not my intention at this time, because of the hour, to go into these routes seriatim. There were two routes which extended from the south shore of lake St. Francis to the

Supply-Transport
city of St. Johns. Consideration was given to a number of other routes, one of them going from Caughnawaga to the Richelieu river and another following the Richelieu river itself.
The point I wish to make at this time is that the international joint commission felt that the time had not arrived to make a determination of the issue and they asked that the matter be held in abeyance, that the report which they made in 1937 be considered as an interim report and that as and when the great lakes-St. Lawrence seaway was developed the international joint commission should be seized of the problem again.
It is quite clear why the international joint commission made that decision. At that time consideration was being given to the great lakes-St. Lawrence waterway. It was inconceivable that this cut-off should be built when so many discussions and so many negotiations had been carried on in connection with the other project. But now that the other project is in fact completed; now that the official opening will take place; now that we know what is going to happen I think the time has arrived first for the appointment of a board of engineers to consider the economics of the Champlain-Richelieu cut-off and, next for referring the matter to the international joint commission so that it might give the proper consideration to it.
The Minister of Transport or the government might feel that the international joint commission is the body itself to appoint the engineers to deal with the matter. But to my mind there is no doubt that the time has now arrived to give this matter consideration. I say that the time has now arrived to give this matter consideration because of the fact that a board of engineers dealing with a matter such as this will take many months, perhaps a year to report; I do not know how long they might take. Because of that fact I think the government should be giving the matter more active consideration.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to call it six o'clock.
Progress reported.
